The method is based on spectral analysis of the three-point function $\langle \mathcal{O}_I \mathcal{E} \mathcal{O}_J\rangle$, where the $\mathcal{O}_I$ are relevant operators and $\mathcal{E}$ is the averaged null energy. This three-point function is decomposed under the spectrum of null rotations that fix the light ray, leading to a positivity condition at each impact parameter.

papers.title: Localizing the M-Theory Path Integral: Membrane Instantons
papers.abstract: We propose a formula for M2-instanton contributions to the M-theory path integral, incorporating quantum corrections to all orders in the Planck length. The M2-brane action is determined by relative equivariant localization, while an equivariant Dolbeault character computes the one-loop determinant. Continuous families of M2-branes are treated by equivariant localization on their moduli spaces. For M-theory backgrounds dual to ABJM theory, we compute single instanton contributions from linear holomorphic fillings to the sphere partition function and the topologically twisted index associated with supersymmetric $AdS_4$ black holes. Our results reproduce known field theory instanton coefficients and give new analytic predictions for mass and squashing deformations at all Chern-Simons levels. For the $V^{5,2}$ theory, we compute new instanton contributions and establish an exact relation between its partition function at special squashing and that of ABJM theory on the round three-sphere.

papers.title: Steerability in top quark decays at the LHC
papers.abstract: Quantum information observables in top quark pair production have opened a new experimental window on non-classical correlations of particle interactions at colliders. Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) steering occupies a distinguished place in the quantum hierarchy, lying between entanglement and Bell nonlocality. We present a detailed collider analysis of steerability for top quark pairs at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). In particular, we utilize both the decay and kinematic methods to estimate the expected sensitivity of the LHC and High Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) to detect steerable states. We find that with the current LHC dataset of $139~\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ the steerability of the $t\bar t$ state in the boosted region can be established at $7.7σ$ ($1.8σ$) in the semileptonic (dileptonic) channel with the decay method, corresponding to a measurement of the steerability integral at a precision of $1.5\%$ ($5.2\%$), while the kinematic method reaches a precision of $0.05\%$ in both channels. At the HL-LHC the decay-method precision improves to $0.3\%$ ($1.1\%$). Near threshold, where the inclusive selections used for entanglement and discord yield a state at the steerability boundary, an optimized selection $M_{t\bar{t}}\lesssim360$--$400$~GeV isolates a steerable singlet-dominated state, where the sensitivity is projected to reach $7σ$ ($3.4σ$). We also provide a detailed discussion on the interpretation of these results with respect to fictitious quantum states, and argue for the robust nature of the steerability measurement at colliders.

papers.title: JWST Observations of Starbursts: Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons in the NGC 253 Superwind
papers.abstract: We present the first spatially resolved study of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) evolution in the galactic superwind of the nearby (d~3.5Mpc) galaxy NGC 253. Using JWST MIRI and NIRCam, we image ~$\pm$2kpc along the galaxy minor axis, capturing both sides of the starburst-driven wind at ~0.05''-0.375'' (~0.85-6.4pc) resolution and providing one of the most detailed views of the wind to date. We target PAH emission at 3.3um, 7.7um, and 11.3um, revealing PAH-bright filamentary streamers along the limb-brightened edges of the outflow cones out to at least a deprojected distance r~0.5kpc, beyond which they likely become confused with the spiral arms. In the southwest (SW) and northeast (NE) streamers, PAH intensity declines faster than $r^{-2}$, suggesting either PAH destruction or a decrease in gas column density or dust-to-gas ratio rather than a response to declining illumination alone. Band ratios trace changes in PAH properties, with the 11.3/7.7um ratio increasing with distance in the SW and northwest (NW) streamers and 3.3/7.7um and 3.3/11.3um decreasing in the SW and NE streamers, indicating larger, more neutral PAHs farther from the starburst. Given the thermal and dynamical properties of the gas in the SW streamer, cool gas is expected to survive acceleration in the outflow and enable PAH shielding. Compared with those of the prototypical starburst M82, the NGC 253 band ratios indicate faster evolution in PAH size. Thus, the NGC 253 wind may represent an earlier stage of outflow evolution in which small PAHs are destroyed near the starburst within the first few Myr.

papers.title: Exact Solutions to Matrix Models and String Theories: The Global Construction
papers.abstract: Exact nonperturbative solutions to matrix models and string theories are obtained in closed-form via a discrete-Fourier/Zak-transform representation of their partition-function resurgent-transseries. Examples include all hermitian one-matrix models (paired with their topological string duals) alongside all their multicritical and minimal-string double-scaling limits. The resulting structure is resonant, necessarily including both eigenvalues (D-branes) and anti-eigenvalues (negative-tension-branes). In a complementary preceding paper these solutions were extensively verified at the local level. In order to study them globally across their phase diagrams, complete non-linear Stokes data (and corresponding connection formulae) are still needed -- all of which are obtained herein. This involves a careful study of (anti-) eigenvalue tunneling across the complete multi-sheeted structure of their associated spectral-curves, and how the result descends from multi-cut smooth-curves to single-cut singular-curves -- all of which are extensively checked via large-order analysis and matrix-integral computations. Making use of the resulting exact Stokes automorphisms, nonperturbative solutions can be fully tested, from weak-to-strong 't Hooft coupling, as well as from large-to-small N, and for any complex-values of all parameters, by correctly implementing Stokes-transitions at the crossing of all possible Stokes-lines. Several analytical and numerical tests are carried through in diverse examples covering from matrix models through non-critical strings, which produce very sharp numerical matches fully validating our exact analytical expressions. Anti-eigenvalues or negative-tension D-branes are an absolutely essential part of the story in order to find such precise agreements.

papers.title: Training Language Models for Introspective Oversight
papers.abstract: Language models increasingly exhibit behaviors that are difficult to detect in transcripts, such as reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy. Asking the assistant follow-up questions about its actions is unreliable, since models are generally not trained to report their own misbehavior. As a result, approaches to oversight typically involve querying external models. These face limitations: external transcript monitoring operates only on visible model outputs, and activation decoders lack full context and are prone to confabulation. We introduce introspective oversight, which trains a new role in the model to answer arbitrary questions about the assistant, rewarding answers that are verified against the assistant's actual behavior. We implement this by adding a separate, third-person observer role that answers these queries, which we can train solely for accuracy and separately from the assistant. On five held-out oversight evaluations, an observer trained on Qwen3.6-27B obtains a mean AUROC of 0.907, outperforming honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.796). We further find that training an observer makes the assistant itself easier to monitor, with every baseline method improving on average when applied to the fine-tuned assistant. These results suggest that training models to answer verifiable questions about themselves is a tractable approach to overseeing unintended behavior.

papers.title: Neural Circuit Architectural Priors for Rat Locomotion
papers.abstract: Animals generate behavior through continuous interactions between their neural circuits, bodies, and environment. Embodied simulations study these interactions by testing neural circuit models in biologically realistic settings. Recent efforts have simulated diverse animals, and emerging work on biologically grounded neural architectures has begun to integrate circuit connectivity and single-unit dynamics from experimental data into artificial neural networks, introducing stronger inductive biases and closer mechanistic alignment with biology. How can we develop embodied simulations that enable the study of increasingly complex bodies and neural circuits? In this work, we address the challenge through coordinated advances in the simulated body, neural architecture, and training infrastructure. We introduce Rat v2, an efficient and flexible biomechanical body for simulating rat behavior. To control this body, we develop Rat NCAP, a biologically grounded neural architecture for locomotion based on mammalian spinal circuits that incorporates cell-type-specific connectivity and a novel flexor-extensor neuromechanical interface. To optimize circuit parameters, we develop GPU-accelerated simulation and training infrastructure. The model learns to locomote at different speeds and transition between gaits without imitation learning, producing locomotion statistics, kinematics, and cell-type-specific neural activity consistent with experimental data. Analyses reveal that the neuromechanical interface substantially affects trainability and gait quality, and in silico cell-type ablations reproduce known gait phenotypes and predict gait changes under graded perturbations. Together, these findings support the view that embodied simulations at an intermediate level of abstraction can simultaneously reproduce complex behavior and yield mechanistic insights into the neural circuits that generate it.

papers.title: Image Watermarking With Memory Across Reissuance
papers.abstract: Publishers often revise and reissue images, yet valid watermarks may persist on superseded releases or unapproved edits. Even a current release can contain regions last authorized at different revisions. We introduce and formalize reissuable provenance: determining an image's current, superseded, or unissued status and recovering each region's last authorized revision (its generation), with abstention when evidence is insufficient. Generational Stratigraphy Fields (GSF) combine watermark evidence with an authenticated live reference to the current release, enabling replacement or retirement without rewriting circulated copies. Each reissue freshly embeds new generation labels in approved regions and inherited labels elsewhere, preserving history without requiring old watermarks to survive successive edits. Our complete-output reissuance evaluation follows 480 histories through four releases, retaining each AI editor's entire output. GSF achieves 99.67% accuracy in classifying issued images as current or superseded and 94.09% recall of unissued edits. After three reissues, one generation map provides time and location: it recovers regional labels with 93.13% median accuracy and localizes the latest approved revision with 92.86% IoU. Regional labels remain readable under tested delivery transformations that impair issued-state recognition. Watermarks can thus express who issued an image, which release is authoritative now, and when each region was last authorized.

papers.title: TRACE-MAS: Diagnosing and Repairing Collaboration Failures in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on not only individual agent behaviors but also the interactions that connect agents, including message exchanges and task dependencies. Existing MAS safeguards mainly perform agent-level anomaly detection, which becomes insufficient when failures originate from agent interactions and detected anomalies do not necessarily reveal their true sources. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{TRACE-MAS}, a finer-grained framework for diagnosing and repairing MAS failures. TRACE-MAS learns normal collaborative execution patterns from benign trajectories and detects deviations in agent state changes, message transitions, and task dependency evolutions. It further identifies responsible execution elements through source-aware attribution and selects minimal interventions to restore collaboration while preserving task-critical capabilities. Experiments on five MAS benchmarks demonstrate that TRACE-MAS significantly improves root-cause localization accuracy by \textbf{60.2}\% and achieves consistent gains in task recovery over strong MAS safeguards.

papers.title: A Survey on the Use of Machine Learning within Computer Algebra
papers.abstract: This survey explores the use of Machine Learning (ML) in the field of Computer Algebra (CA), both to optimise existing CA algorithms, and to perform symbolic computation directly. Traditional symbolic methods, while mathematically rigorous, often are computationally expensive thus limiting their use in real-world applications. Recent advances have shown that data-driven techniques can address these limitations by guiding heuristic decisions, selecting optimal algorithms, predicting structural properties of algebraic objects, or even making direct symbolic computations. We take a systematic literature review approach and uncover work in CA applications including cylindrical algebraic decomposition, Gröbner basis computation, symbolic integration, and many more. The survey compares the different ML approaches that have been employed for these tasks, ranging from decision trees to transformers. Issues uncovered by the survey include the lack of benchmark datasets for CA, which hinders the comparison of methods and the generalizability of ML models. The survey identifies the potential for explainable AI tools to help develop trust in decisions, and to drive forward CA research itself.

papers.title: A Minimal Toy Model of Charged Superradiant Spin-Down in Extreme-Mass-Ratio Inspirals
papers.abstract: Long-lived extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) are sensitive to slow changes in the mass and spin of their central black holes. We construct a deliberately minimal toy model in which an effective hidden charge opens a charged-superradiance channel, a bosonic cloud grows from a seed, and energy and angular momentum are transferred from a rotating black hole to the cloud. The model is not a Kerr-Newman perturbation calculation. Instead, it consists of a threshold function, one phenomenological rate coefficient, and balance equations that conserve the combined black-hole-cloud energy. This reduction yields an analytic relation between mass loss and spin-down and makes the roles of the growth coefficient, seed energy, and superradiant margin transparent. For an illustrative system with initial mass $2\times10^6 M_\odot$, spin 0.90, effective charge-to-mass ratio 0.30, and a one-year evolution time, the chosen benchmark reaches $M/M_0=0.8933$ and $a_\star=0.7704$. These values are then passed to FastEMRIWaveforms as two stationary Kerr snapshots. The resulting figures show that the endpoint state has a shifted time-domain oscillation pattern and a lower-frequency harmonic structure relative to the initial state. Because the snapshots are regenerated independently, they do not constitute a phase-connected, time-dependent waveform and cannot by themselves support a detectability claim. The value of the construction is instead diagnostic: it isolates a compact set of assumptions, exposes parameter degeneracies, and identifies the minimum ingredients required for a future self-consistent calculation. In this sense, the model provides a reproducible bridge between charged-superradiance intuition and EMRI waveform studies without presenting its benchmark as an astrophysical forecast.

papers.title: Prioritize, Don't Decide: What We Learned Auditing a Deployed Human-in-the-Loop CV Sorter
papers.abstract: A single academic vacancy can draw hundreds of applications, and the first screening round consumes most of a committee's time. We describe a CV Priority Sorter deployed at a national platform for academic vacancies and integrated with its vacancy database. It proposes a reading order for a pile of CVs and leaves every decision to the committee, pairing a frozen multilingual transformer encoder with a per-session linear model that retrains after each label and is discarded when the session ends. It works: on a pool of 300 synthetic CVs, a committee reading in the tool's order reaches 95% of the relevant candidates after half the pile, where an arbitrary order needs almost all of it. This paper is about what we found when we audited that claim, rather than about the system itself. Three findings changed the product. The pool turned out to be sortable by document length alone, which makes precision-style metrics on it uninformative; regenerating it under a shared length budget removes that shortcut and leaves the reading-depth result standing. The four-level agreement score such systems report, ours included, is a binary probability cut at fixed thresholds, so it follows the classifier's confidence rather than its ranking and falls as labels accumulate. And uncertainty sampling, the obvious way to implement a "suggest the next CV" button, leaves model quality intact but raises the committee's total reading load above the no-label baseline, because the CVs it asks about are the ones that would otherwise be skipped. A fourth result shows where to look next: a hosted LLM embedding model lifts zero-label ordinal discrimination from 0.66 to 0.80 under length control, then stops mattering once the session model has two dozen labels; a local cross-encoder matches that cold-start gain without sending data out. We report the fixes each finding forced.

papers.title: Implementing Binary Transformers with Approximate Memories with Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) Protection
papers.abstract: Quantization is an effective technique to reduce memory storage, computation complexity and power for Transformers, and the binarization of the weights is important for meeting these requirements. Approximate memory can further reduce the power for memory, but it also introduces errors. Current research for binary Transformers focuses on task performance, but the model dependable operation against errors on the memory has not been well studied. In this paper, we first evaluate the dependability of binary Transformers with the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) as a case study. A large accuracy loss occurs only at high Bit Error Rates (e.g. BER = 5% or 10%). Then we propose a novel Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) scheme to protect the binary weights at very low overhead. This scheme exploits the invariance of Transformers to permutations in the rows and columns to group the critical weights and perform selective protection on those weights. Simulation results show that PIES can recover most of the performance loss caused by bit errors at BERs as high as 10%, at an overhead significantly lower than traditional error correction schemes. These results confirm the feasibility of running binary Transformers using approximate memory with aggressive voltage scaling on resource-limited low power edge devices. The code for PIES is released on github (https://github.com/YangZhutian/binary-transformer-prefix-repair).

papers.title: A Survey on RLOps for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become increasingly important for improving the reasoning, instruction-following, and task-solving capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, scaling RL training exposes failures in distributed execution, feedback computation, and learning dynamics that can waste computational resources, slow training, and undermine model improvements. These challenges have motivated a growing body of techniques for LLM RLOps, which manages the efficiency and reliability of operations throughout the LLM reinforcement learning training lifecycle. Despite growing interest, these techniques remain scattered across research areas, with limited synthesis of their operational roles and interactions. To bridge this gap, we present a systematic survey of LLM RLOps methods. We organize existing approaches into five stages: Training Setup, Experience Collection, Reward Computation, Policy Optimization, and Model Evaluation. Within each stage, we examine operational concerns, management techniques, and evaluation evidence. Building on this taxonomy, we identify open challenges and future directions in training process observability, cross-stage coordination, generalizable RLOps, multi-run management, and RLOps for recursive self-improvement. These directions extend operational management from individual training runs to diverse training settings, shared infrastructure, and successive improvement cycles. We maintain a GitHub repository indexing relevant papers and open resources at https://github.com/zhanglingzhe0820/Awesome-RLOps.

papers.title: Theta-Eta Mellin Transforms, Shifted Reflections, and Rigorous Approximation Theory for a Variant Theta Construction
papers.abstract: We develop a rigorous analytic framework for investigating a proposed functional equation associated with a variant theta construction. We prove the classical Mellin identity connecting the Jacobi kernel $1-θ_4(0\mid ix^2)$ to the completed Dirichlet eta function, and extend its Mellin transform meromorphically to the whole plane with a single simple pole at the origin. Mellin uniqueness identifies $x^{3/8}(1-θ_4(0\mid ix^2))$ as the unique kernel in a natural weighted $L^1$ class whose Mellin transform is the shifted completed eta function. We distinguish this Gaussian kernel from the weighted exponential series $Θ^B(s)=\sum_{n\geq1}ne^{-ns}$, whose Mellin transform is $Γ(s)ζ(s-1)$ and obeys a different, explicitly derived reflection relation. We show that every affine reflection $s\mapsto c-s$ can be generated for a shifted completed eta or zeta function by choosing the shift appropriately; consequently, the occurrence of $\tfrac14-s$ alone cannot identify the original variant with a shifted eta function. The corrected analytic product defined here is an elementary meromorphic multiplier of the completed zeta function and therefore has a precise $1-s$ functional equation. We prove an explicit eta-tail bound, a sharper alternating-tail asymptotic, a uniformly convergent Euler-transformed eta series with a geometric error bound, a uniform zeta-approximation bound away from the line $\Re s=1$, and a combined truncation estimate when both the zeta and weighted-exponential factors are truncated. We also determine the principal Laurent data and the cancellation of the gamma poles at the trivial zeta zeros for the corrected product. Reproducible high-precision experiments verify the stated error scales. The exact identification of the original variant with a shifted completed eta function remains open.

papers.title: Isospin effects and symmetry energy in nuclear reactions
papers.abstract: Isospin and the symmetry energy are linked within the symmetry term of the liquid-drop mass formula and within the corresponding term of the equation of state of asymmetric nuclear matter. The Pauli exclusion principle leads to a leading quadratic dependence of the kinetic part of the symmetry term of the nuclear binding-energy formula on the neutron-proton asymmetry (N-Z)/A. Charge symmetry ensures the same leading quadratic dependence for the potential part. Charge invariance further generalizes this dependence, to lowest order, from T$_3^2$ to T(T+1). The strength of the symmetry term, in contrast, is determined by the symmetry energy. At sub-saturation densities the symmetry energy can be constrained by nuclear-structure observables, such as neutron skin thicknesses, isovector collective modes and the related electric dipole polarizability, and excitation energies of isobaric analog states. It can also be constrained by reaction observables, such as charge exchange and elastic scattering cross sections, isoscaling and isospin diffusion. At supra-saturation densities, by contrast, the only means of studying asymmetric nuclear matter under laboratory conditions are relativistic heavy-ion collisions. These studies use differential observables such as neutron/proton flows and light isobar or $π^{-}/π^{+}$ ratios. Complementary information can be obtained from neutron star observations including gravitational waves. The latest measurements and analyses of the stiffness of the symmetry energy will be presented, together with the recent NA61/SHINE observation of an unexpectedly large isospin-symmetry violation in kaon production. Attention will also be paid to the challenges of measuring charged and neutral products of relativistic heavy-ion collisions in the context of the recent ASY-EOS II experiment at GSI and to the new detectors used in the setup.

papers.title: AI, Specialization, and the Organization of Knowledge Work: Evidence from Legal Services
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence makes specialized knowledge cheaper to use, but its effects on professional-service firms depend on how clients reallocate work and how suppliers respond. We develop a framework linking individual self-provision, enterprise make-or-buy decisions, and pricing by specialist firms. As AI improves lower-priced alternatives, clients may reallocate work across outside providers without bringing it in-house. If the departing work is more price-sensitive than the work that remains, premium firms may raise their optimal markups even as their share of work declines. We examine these margins in U.S. legal services. Across 89 federal districts, a difference-in-differences analysis finds a 6.6-percentage-point increase in non-prisoner self-representation relative to prisoner petitions by fiscal 2025, remaining substantial after adjusting for pre-existing trends. In contrast, lawyer employment shows no clear post-2022 shift toward client firms. Legal-AI benchmarks reveal continuing limitations in reliably completing complex, multi-step work, offering one possible explanation. Meanwhile, the largest law firms reported 13% revenue growth in 2025 despite nearly flat billable hours, while lower-priced firms experienced stronger demand growth. Reported AI integration is also stronger among firms with lower revenue per lawyer. These patterns highlight the importance of changes in work allocation and supplier competition, even as much of the underlying reallocation predates generative AI. The findings illustrate why cheaper expertise need not produce either widespread internalization or declining prices for premium professional services.

papers.title: Idempotency Is Not Recovery: A Fault-Injection Study of Language-Model Agent Tool Actions
papers.abstract: When a language-model agent's tool call is interrupted, the action may already have changed an external system without confirmation. Retrying risks duplication; assuming success may conceal an action that never occurred. We study these failure modes in a controlled agent runtime combining authorization, an action ledger, target-side idempotency, reconciliation, and evidence sealing. We inject ten single-host fault classes and compare four configurations and three ablations using a target-side oracle separate from the runtime ledger. On each of Windows and Linux, 7,513 trials used 96 captured model responses from 24 constructed cases. In 200 known original crash and replay pairs, the full configuration recorded 0/200 repeated effects versus 117/200 for each simpler baseline. A ledger-related ablation had 170/170 orphaned effects versus 0/170 and 200/300 recovery successes versus 300/300 for the full configuration. Disabling reconciliation left 100/100 known post-effect crash outcomes ambiguous despite no observed duplicates. A separate supplement designed after the initial results and reusing the same inputs found a similar pattern under response loss or delay. The full runtime had about one-seventh of fail-open throughput, while injected evidence-write faults left 75/100 trials per platform unresolved. These findings distinguish duplicate suppression from recovery and identify their measured reliability and performance tradeoffs within the tested benchmark.

papers.title: Streaming Generative Video Compression with Embedding Alignment and In-Context Propagation
papers.abstract: Video compression at ultra-low bitrates presents substantial challenges in preserving perceptual quality. Although pretrained video diffusion transformers (DiTs) provide powerful generative priors, existing generative video compression (GVC) methods built on them typically rely on computationally expensive VAE decoders to reconstruct video frames. Moreover, jointly refining multiple frames to exploit the inherent spatiotemporal modeling capabilities of video DiTs introduces additional buffering delay. To address these challenges, we propose SGVC, a streaming generative video compression framework that adapts a pretrained latent video DiT into a causal pixel-space refiner. Specifically, SGVC projects decoded features from a contextual pixel codec directly into the DiT input embedding space. To bridge the representation gap between codec-derived embeddings and pretrained DiT embeddings, we introduce Embedding Alignment, which aligns the projected embeddings with input embeddings extracted from the original frames during training. The refined DiT hidden states are then mapped directly to the pixel domain through a lightweight reconstruction path, bypassing the pretrained VAE decoder. To further exploit the spatiotemporal priors of the video DiT while maintaining causal decoding, we introduce In-Context Propagation, which reuses layer-wise K/V states across frames to exploit historical generative context, improving temporal consistency without requiring clip-wise buffering. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SGVC achieves competitive rate-perception performance, with average BD-rate savings of 71.97% over S$^2$VC in terms of DISTS. Project Page: https://chigland.github.io/SGVC/

papers.title: SWIMSS: An Open Multi-Center SwinUNETR Model for Multiple Sclerosis White Matter Lesion Segmentation
papers.abstract: Purpose: To develop and validate SWIMSS (SWInUNETR for Multiple Sclerosis white matter lesion Segmentation), a SwinUNETR-based deep learning (DL) model for reliable automated white matter (WM) lesion segmentation, in a large multicentric cohort of people with multiple sclerosis (pwMS). Methods: A real-world longitudinal dataset of 1,385 pwMS from seven Swiss clinical centers was used to train, validate, and test SWIMSS and two state-of-the-art DL architectures: UNETR and MSSegDiff. Inference results obtained with LST-AI were also compared. Preprocessed magnetization-prepared rapid acquisition gradient echo and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery MRI sequences, acquired with various MR systems and field strengths, served as model inputs. Model performance was evaluated using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results: SWIMSS achieved the highest performance, with a DSC of 81.37 (95% CI: 80.63-82.11), outperforming UNETR (79.06; 95% CI: 78.33-79.79), MSSegDiff (75.70; 95% CI: 74.97-76.43), and LST-AI (63.19; 95% CI: 62.08-64.30). Normalized DSC followed a similar trend, with SWIMSS reaching 84.88. Lesion detection F1 achieved 81.14. Statistical analyses confirmed its superior performance (p < 0.001). Conclusion: SWIMSS achieved state-of-the-art performance for WM lesion segmentation. By making this model publicly available, we enable broader access to high-quality segmentation tools, allowing smaller centers, often lacking large annotated datasets or computational resources, to benefit from a model trained on a diverse, large-scale cohort. This promotes more equitable access to advanced imaging analysis and supports reproducibility and standardization in MS research.

papers.title: Asymmetric Optical Image Watermarking
papers.abstract: Watermark detectors held by a provider cannot be checked by third parties, and a party that can detect a mark can usually also forge it. We study a two-layer image watermark in which the Fourier transform at the core of the pipeline is performed by a coherent optical 4F unit. Layer 1 carries an Ed25519 signature bound to the image content in Fourier magnitudes, so anyone with the public key verifies offline. Layer 2 is a key-defined carrier written by a secret phase hologram and read by a matched-filter correlator. The optics is a scalar-diffraction simulation with finite modulator bits, pixel aperture, pupil, defocus, misalignment, and sensor noise. No hardware is built. All criteria were fixed in a hashed specification before any optical result. The simulated optical signer reproduces the digital pipeline (field error 1.7e-15, bit agreement 99.997%), verifies at least 99.5% of 877 images under each of 8 post-sensor settings, one unattacked, and accepts none of 40,670 unmarked images. The optical carrier is key-selective: the matched key detects it on 99.8% of the unattacked images, and detection falls to 0% under a scale error of 1% and to 0% under a mask shift of 1 bin. Security rests on the signature and the content binding, for which we separate what is provable from what is measured.

papers.title: Systematic Mapping Protocol. Generative AI-Augmented Requirements Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study of Practices, Specifications, and Reuse in Software Development
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly large language models (LLMs), is rapidly being adopted in requirements engineering (RE). Existing secondary studies have characterized which RE activities are supported and which prompting strategies are used, but little is known about the specifications that GenAI-augmented RE produces and how they are used in subsequent activities such as specification-driven development (SDD), design and code generation, test derivation, verification, and reuse. This document presents the protocol of a systematic mapping study (SMS) that will identify and classify research on GenAI-augmented RE, with particular attention to the work products it generates and their downstream use. The protocol defines the research questions and their classification schemes, the search strategy, the study selection procedure, the data extraction form, the analysis approach, the tool support, and the threats to validity. It is published in advance to establish a prior commitment and to support the transparency and repeatability of the study.

papers.title: SIGMA: speaker-isolated, symptom-structured multimodal estimation of depression severity from clinical interviews
papers.abstract: Clinical interviews are central to depression assessment but time-consuming and rater-dependent. Automated severity estimation offers scalable screening, yet existing methods often retain interviewer speech (confounding participant cues), fuse modalities late (losing fine-grained cross-modal dynamics), or score symptoms independently (ignoring inter-symptom correlations). We present SIGMA, a speaker-aware, symptom-structured framework for depression-severity estimation from semi-clinical interviews. SIGMA uses speaker diarization to restrict input to participant speech, cross-attention so that text, audio and video condition one another during encoding, and a graded-response head that predicts the eight questionnaire items jointly through a shared latent severity trait with item-specific ordered thresholds. On the Extended Distress Analysis Interview Corpus, SIGMA achieves state-of-the-art performance (CCC 0.762, RMSE 4.13, MAE 3.30 over five seeds). Ablations confirm that isolating participant speech and joint, structured symptom prediction each substantially improve concordance and estimation accuracy.

papers.title: SurgCBVR: A Multi-Domain Benchmark for Content-Based Surgical Video-to-Video Retrieval
papers.abstract: Hospitals record thousands of hours of surgical video annually, yet these archives remain difficult to search by content. Surgeons cannot readily retrieve similar operations, complications, or workflow events. Existing surgical computer vision primarily produces labels rather than retrieving relevant videos. We introduce SurgCBVR, the first benchmark for content-based video-to-video retrieval in surgery. It integrates eight public datasets across four domains-ophthalmic, laparoscopic, robotic-assisted, and colonoscopy-covering six procedure types, 679 cases, and 76,489 clips (106 hours). SurgCBVR comprises two tiers: Scene, retrieving the same operative state across cases and sites, and Workflow, retrieving and localizing phase transitions and deviations. Scene includes 74,765 clips spanning 40 classes, three temporal granularities, and three playback speeds; Workflow contains 1,724 transition clips. Fixed clip lengths and frame counts, together with phase-classifier oracle and duration-only baselines, help assess label and timing shortcuts. We evaluate six generic and surgical foundation models, two video retrieval methods, and contrastive heads trained on SurgCBVR, using within-dataset, cross-dataset, and pooled-gallery retrieval restricted to the same procedure type. Frozen representations barely outperform a timing-only baseline, transition retrieval approaches chance, and trained heads lose up to half their accuracy across datasets. These findings expose substantial limitations in current video representations and establish SurgCBVR as a benchmark for advancing surgery-aware retrieval.

papers.title: Securing and Auditing Long-Horizon LLM Agents: State-Transfer Auditing and Controls in the Agent Harness
papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents across codebases, web browsers, and enterprise infrastructure rely on an execution harness to move state between the working context, session history, persistent memory, and external environment. While conventional execution traces log model prompts and tool calls, critical security and reliability failures occur during state transfers: a transfer can admit unchecked content (indirect prompt injections, unverified memory writes), rewrite state lossily (context compaction dropping user constraints, memory consolidation stripping source authority), or restore state incompletely (workspace rollbacks leaving aborted KV state active on the inference server). Because current traces omit what crosses these boundaries, failure attribution and runtime monitors fail on multi-step trajectories. We present a state-transfer audit architecture for the agent harness. At each transfer boundary, we define an audit point specifying the minimal hash-chained record the harness emits, separating low-overhead deterministic checks from model-based semantic checks and binding internal context, memory, and inference-server cache state to external actions. We show that the same transfer records required for causal failure attribution supply the durable state needed by runtime security controls, including least-privilege capabilities, replay-resistant authorization outside the prompt, information flow control, obligation monitors, and transactional recovery across multi-agent and infrastructure pipelines. Finally, we analyze multimodal GUI adaptations and implement and evaluate a reference harness middleware across 240 multi-step fault-injection trajectories, showing that transfer records localize root causes and catch cross-transfer violations missed by lifecycle and tool-only logs at microsecond deterministic overhead.

papers.title: BiMa-ECGSR: reconstructing the 12-lead ECG from reduced lead sets with bidirectional state-space models
papers.abstract: Wearables and monitors record few electrocardiogram (ECG) leads; most diagnostic tools assume 12 leads. BiMa-ECGSR reconstructs the 12-lead ECG from reduced lead sets with a bidirectional Mamba state-space encoder--decoder, as regression (BiMa-SR) or diffusion (DiBiMa-SR). Models were trained on PTB-XL for six input sets (I; II; I+II; I+II+V1; I+II+V2; I+II+V1+V4), see only the measured leads at inference, and were tested on the PTB-XL test fold (2,198 records) and two external cohorts (Georgia, 10,275 records; Chapman-Shaoxing/Ningbo, 43,559). From lead II alone, the pooled median Pearson correlation (PCC) over the 11 predicted leads was 0.914 on PTB-XL, against 0.784 for a least-squares linear filter (lead I: 0.906 against 0.789). As limb leads are exactly derivable from I and II, multi-lead inputs were compared on predicted chest leads: 0.939 against 0.849 for I+II and 0.979 against 0.962 for I+II+V1+V4. BiMa-SR exceeded the linear comparator in all 18 configuration--cohort pairs (by 0.012--0.136), a margin that shrank as chest leads were added. From lead II, regression was more accurate than diffusion (DiBiMa-SR: 0.903 one-step, 0.862 with six DDIM steps). A 12-lead classifier trained only on real ECGs reached a superclass macro AUROC of 0.912 on real PTB-XL ECGs, 0.843 on reconstructions from lead II and 0.908 from I+II+V1+V4; externally, reconstructions from three or four leads scored within 0.004 of real ECGs. BiMa-SR (2.68\,M parameters) takes 45.8 ms per 10-s record on a GPU. Reconstruction makes reduced-lead recordings usable by 12-lead tools; it cannot add information absent from the measured leads.

papers.title: Beyond Accuracy: Benchmarking Uncertainty Quantification in Retinal Disease Screening
papers.abstract: Reliable uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for evaluating retinal AI systems beyond classification accuracy, yet it remains unclear whether existing UQ strategies generalize across diseases, model architectures, and reliability criteria. We introduce a large-scale, multi-disease benchmark comprising over $242,000$ fundus photographs from $32$ datasets covering diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, and glaucoma. We evaluate six representative UQ strategies across three Vision Transformer configurations, assessing discrimination, probabilistic calibration, selective prediction, and conformal prediction-set coverage. Our findings reveal no universally superior model or UQ strategy: methods that improve reliability in one disease or architecture may underperform in another, while improvements in discrimination, calibration, and selective prediction do not necessarily align. Notably, computationally intensive methods do not consistently outperform simple confidence scores, and domain-specific foundation models and calibration-oriented loss functions do not guarantee greater reliability. In contrast, conformal prediction provides a complementary framework for achieving near-nominal marginal prediction-set coverage across diverse settings, subject to its statistical assumptions. These findings challenge universal UQ recommendations and highlight the need for disease-specific, model-specific, and multidimensional reliability evaluation before clinical deployment. We release standardized dataset splits, trained checkpoints, evaluation code, and an interactive research demonstration to support reproducible benchmarking.

papers.title: An energy-dependent rescaling of the neutrino propagation Hamiltonian: Standard Model Extension identification, matter sector, and long-baseline degeneracy
papers.abstract: We study the consequences of multiplying the neutrino propagation Hamiltonian by a real, energy-dependent scalar, $H_η(E)=f(E)H_0(E)$ with $f(E)=1-η_0(E/E_0)^2$, a minimal-length ansatz. Its vacuum part is a dimension-four, CPT-even Lorentz-violating term of the Standard Model Extension with coefficient $(\cL)_{ii}=-η_0(m_i^2-m_1^2)/(2E_0^2)$, diagonal in the mass basis and fixed by the mass matrix, hence removable by a reparametrization. The matter-potential rescaling has dimension-five behaviour and is CPT-odd. For $f=1-η_0(E/E_0)^p$ the vacuum term behaves as a dimension $p+2$ operator and the matter term as $p+3$, so only $p=2$ gives a marginal vacuum operator; $p=0$ is absorbed into the measured mass splittings, and non-integer $p$ admits no local operator. For $η_0=0.02$ at $E_0=2.5$~GeV we find $|(\cL)_{33}|\simeq4\times10^{-24}$, comparable to present atmospheric bounds, whereas a Planck-suppressed deformation with $β_0=\mathcal{O}(1)$ gives $3.2\times10^{-58}$. At constant density it is equivalent to $L\to f(E)L$: mixing angles and the Dirac phase are unchanged, the CP asymmetry is reparametrized rather than generated, and the leading observable is a rescaling of $\dm_{31}$. At $1297$~km a re-fit of $\dm_{31}$ alone absorbs $23$~per cent of the squared probability difference, and a four-parameter re-fit absorbs $41.5$~per cent. No statistical analysis is performed; degeneracy means a distance in probability space, not a confidence interval.

papers.title: Confidence-Based Materials Data Quality Assessment via Domain Knowledge and Graph-Structured Learning
papers.abstract: The rapid development of materials machine learning relies on large-scale, heterogeneous datasets, yet model reliability is often compromised by imperfect data from diverse experiments, simulations, and database integration. Real-world materials databases may contain measurement errors, failed calculations, missing or duplicate records, and hidden violations of physicochemical constraints. Such problems are difficult to identify because corrupted samples may remain statistically plausible rather than appearing as explicit outliers. In this paper, we propose a confidence-based materials data quality assessment framework that integrates domain knowledge with graph-structured learning. Data quality is formulated as a continuous confidence estimation problem rather than a binary anomaly identification task, enabling sample-level assessment and historical-reference-based batch comparison. A nine-dimensional feature-quality prior and duplicate-aware sample initialization are calibrated using materials domain rules and statistical evidence. Confidence is further refined through sample-feature bipartite graph propagation and weakly supervised graph attention, while a Memory-GAT module provides historical reference scoring. Experiments on 23 ODDS benchmark datasets show that the generic module achieves an average AUC-ROC of 0.866. In five repeated mixed-contamination experiments on mp\_20, rule calibration improves HistGradientBoostingRegressor test $R^2$ from $0.538\pm0.008$ to $0.616\pm0.014$. Graph refinement increases average precision from $0.943\pm0.004$ to 0.953\pm0.004$, while the rule-calibrated configuration has the highest mean test $R^2$ among the evaluated screening configurations. Five repeated MACE subset experiments further show an increase in $R^2$ from $0.590\pm0.053$ to $0.880\pm0.027$ after rule-based screening.

papers.title: Management of Behavioral Addictions via Artificial Intelligence based Digital Technologies
papers.abstract: Behavioral addictions, such as problematic gaming, gambling, social media use, and online shopping, have emerged as a growing global concern with significant psychological, social, and economic consequences. Traditional assessment and treatment approaches, while clinically grounded, often struggle with scalability, accessibility, and long-term engagement. In recent years, advances in digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) have enabled the development of novel, data-driven solutions for the prevention, detection, treatment, and recovery of behavioral addictions. This book presents a comprehensive survey of the management of behavioral addictions through digital technologies, bridging clinical foundations with state-of-the-art computational approaches. This book aims to provide researchers, clinicians, and practitioners with a unified, interdisciplinary perspective on the opportunities and limitations of AI-based digital technologies in behavioral addiction management,and to highlight pathways toward more scalable, personalized, and effective intervention strategies.

papers.title: Thermodynamic Parameterizations of Dark Energy in Light of DESI DR2 BAO
papers.abstract: The physical origin of cosmic acceleration remains one of the central unresolved problems of modern cosmology. Although the $Λ$CDM model successfully describes a wide range of cosmological observations, its interpretation in terms of a strictly constant vacuum energy faces long-standing theoretical challenges, motivating the search for physically grounded alternatives. In this work, we develop a thermodynamic parametrization of dark energy (TPDE) by combining the second law of thermodynamics with the kinematic evolution of the Universe. By imposing physically motivated constraints on the cosmic deceleration parameter and reconstructing its evolution through a Padé approximant, we derive a one-parameter extension of $Λ$CDM in which late-time accelerated expansion emerges from thermodynamic principles rather than an assumed cosmological constant. We constrain the model using Planck 2018 CMB temperature, polarization, and lensing observations, DESI DR2 BAO measurements, and the Pantheon$+$, DES-Dovekie, and Union3 Type Ia supernova compilations. The present-day thermodynamic parameter remains tightly constrained around the $Λ$CDM limit, implying that departures from a cosmological constant are small. While the model does not resolve the $H_0$ tension because it preserves the sound horizon at the drag epoch, it agrees with weak-lensing constraints on $S_8$, with tensions below $0.2σ$ for KiDS-Legacy (Shear) and $1.5σ$ for DES~Y6. Despite maximum-likelihood fits comparable to $Λ$CDM, Bayesian model comparison consistently yields a weak-to-moderate preference for TPDE. These results demonstrate that thermodynamic reconstruction provides a simple, physically motivated, and observationally competitive alternative to $Λ$CDM, offering a framework for investigating the origin of dark energy with forthcoming high-precision cosmological observations.

papers.title: Optimize the Cob, Then the Kernel: Optimizing Beam Search for Generative Recommendation Inference
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) inference differs substantially from conventional LLM serving, featuring long input sequences, wide beam search, and only a few fixed output tokens. Existing LLM serving engines such as vLLM process beams as batched independent sequences, causing redundant KV cache accesses over the shared prompt prefix. Furthermore, vLLM executes each beam search generation step as a separate engine invocation, incurring host-side beam processing overhead between decoding steps and substantial runtime KV block management in PagedAttention. Using Tree Attention, we concatenate beams along the sequence dimension to eliminate redundant KV accesses, and further optimize execution through pre-generated partial-attention masks, static KV cache allocation, loop-unrolled generation dispatch, TorchAir graph compilation, automatic operator fusion, and vocabulary-constrained decoding. Without the use of custom kernels, our approach reduces end-to-end latency by up to 25x over vLLM on Ascend NPUs, and achieves generation latency comparable to a SOTA solution using custom kernels, showing that the generation pipeline should be optimized holistically before resorting to custom kernel development.

papers.title: An Explicit Construction of Large Families of MSTD Sets
papers.abstract: A finite set $S\subset\mathbb Z$ is more sums than differences (MSTD) if $|S+S|>|S-S|$. Yufei Zhao's bidirectional-ballot construction gives $Θ(2^N/N)$ MSTD subsets of $[0,N-1]$, the best previously known size bound for an explicit family, to the author's knowledge. We improve this bound: for every fixed integer $T\geq1$, we construct a family of $Θ_T(2^N/(\log_2^{\circ T} N)^{2^T})$ MSTD subsets, where $\log_2^{\circ T}$ denotes the $T$-fold iterated logarithm. This family is asymptotically larger than Zhao's for every fixed $T\geq1$. A subfamily of the same order of magnitude can be numbered so that any chosen member can be generated deterministically in time polynomial in $N$, without listing preceding members. As a supplementary comparison, replacing the terminal ballot rule by exhaustive fringe search gives a positive-proportion family with the same polynomial-time generation property.

papers.title: Cross-probing van der Waals multiferroics
papers.abstract: Multiferroic materials, with coupled electric and magnetic orders, hold the potential to enable low-power memory and logic devices by replacing electrical currents with electric fields for magnetic switching. Reducing the dimensionality of multiferroics, from 3D to 2D, has opened new frontiers in this already burgeoning field by enabling unprecedented control over magnetoelectric coupling that is beyond the reach of bulk counterparts, owing to reduced electrostatic screening and enhanced quantum fluctuations at the atomically thin limit. A notable example is a few-layer NiI2 multiferroic, which exhibits coexisting chiral spin textures and (anti)ferroelectricity, accompanied by strong magnetoelectric coupling; by simultaneously breaking time-reversal and spatial-inversion symmetry, NiI2 shows new physical properties such as unique mutual control of chiral magnetism and polarization with giant magnetoelectric coupling, ultrafast electromagnon excitations and odd-parity p-wave magnetism. However, there are experimental challenges in unambiguously identifying intrinsic multiferroicity. This Review critically examines the current landscape of 2D multiferroic materials, with an emphasis on experimental methodologies rather than material taxonomy. We assess different conventional probes for magnetism and ferroelectricity and identify key limitations in single-technique approaches. We emphasize the importance of magneto-opto-electric cross-correlative measurements in establishing intrinsic multiferroic behaviour and outline future research directions for both fundamental studies and device applications.

papers.title: RootSink: Reproducible C/C++ Crashes with Tested Repair Sites
papers.abstract: When a C or C++ program crashes on a crafted input, the line that crashes is often not the line that is wrong. Tools and models that repair or locate vulnerabilities need examples showing both, with evidence for each, which existing datasets rarely provide. RootSink provides 3341 records from 354 open-source projects. Most give the crash site a memory-error detector reported and a candidate location for its root cause, and label each with a weakness type and its evidence. For the 1954 records in the Reproduced tier, we re-ran the crash ourselves and confirmed that the fixed version runs cleanly. In 1275 of these, a single hunk of the developer's fix stopped the crash on its own. That marks a tested repair site, though not necessarily the defect, and 1273 records use it as the root. In a blind audit of an earlier version, two co-author raters called 68% and 92% of the tested repair sites they saw the defect, but only 37% and 51% of that version's located Reproduced-tier roots. RootSink ships with tasks, a patch scorer and run logs.

papers.title: Truthgate: Checking Coding Agents Against a Record They Cannot Edit - Cheating, Deterrence and Disclosure on Impossible Tasks
papers.abstract: When a coding agent says it is done, is that true, and how would anyone know? We study this question in five steps; every paid study was pre-registered, and in each step the agent is checked against a record it cannot edit: tests re-run by the host and, from step 2 on, hidden checks in containers the agent never sees and a signed log of every tool call written by a signer outside the agent's sandbox. A pilot with a small local model (Qwen3.5-4B, 36 runs on impossible tasks) found no hidden failure, and showed that labels built from actions alone over-count lies. On Impossible-LiveCodeBench, Claude Sonnet 5.5 passed 39 of 180 impossible tasks (21.7%), every time by special-casing its code to fit the failing assertion; Opus 5.5 (2.8%) and Haiku 5.5 (1.7%) rarely did. One sentence appended to the system prompt cut Sonnet's cheats on the same 60 tasks from 22 to 8 (an AI reviewer will read the transcript), 6 (a person will review the work), 6 ("This session is recorded.") and 1 (do not special-case tests), all significant under exact McNemar tests, with honest passes unchanged. No remaining cheat moved to a shell falsely described as unrecorded (0 of 4). Asked for a final report, every one of 55 natural cheats named its special case; unasked, Sonnet and Opus said nothing in 52 of 52. An LLM judge caught all 55; deterministic rules over the host record caught 27. A scripted tamper demonstration, with keyword stand-ins for the judges, shows that one rewrite of the agent-side transcript hides two calls from a judge that reads it, while the signed record keeps them; in a 40-rollout pilot, Sonnet never touched its transcript. The judge and the record caught different things, which leads to our main conclusion: the record is the evidence a judge should read, not a replacement for one. All pre-registrations, results documents, code and evidence manifests are released.

papers.title: Integrating AI Coding Agents Into Scientific Research
papers.abstract: New software tools have emerged that enable AI agents to quickly develop code that analyzes data and generates figures, but their mistakes can also harm a researcher's computer, require extensive resources for validation, and cause the results to be received more skeptically. These concerns could be mitigated if scientific software is developed in a secure environment with a system for monitoring file changes and well-defined standards for handling AI agents. This paper first describes how coding agents change eleven aspects of generating, verifying, and reproducing numerical results. A six-level scale is then proposed for classifying AI-assisted numerical experiments by their provenance, reproducibility, openness, oversight, and falsifiability (PROOF). The scale begins with locally self-consistent, version-controlled, human-verified results and culminates in a publicly accessible and curated archive of the files, change history, prompt transcripts, independent agent regeneration of the analysis, and multiple cryptographically verifiable attestations of regeneration by independent researchers. These aspects of AI-assisted scientific software development have been synthesized into a new open source software package called vaibify that optimizes the agentic development of computational experiments ascending the PROOF Ladder. Docker containers sequester the agents while a GUI enables researchers to prompt command line agents, monitor the current status of local and remote files, and drive a project to PROOF Level 3 (reproducible). The methods described in this paper could help researchers reduce the time required to verify agent-written software and efficiently communicate trust in AI-assisted science.

papers.title: Classification of Forbidden 0-1 Patterns by Their Extremal Function
papers.abstract: This paper concerns the maximum weight of $n\times n$ 0-1 matrices that avoid some pattern $P$, denoted $\operatorname{ex}(n,P)$. Furedi and Hajnal initiated a research program of classifying all patterns according to their extremal function, but to date, only the weight-4 patterns are completely understood. In this paper we make progress on several fronts of the classification problem. A pattern is light if its columns have weight 1 and linear if $\operatorname{ex}(n,P)=O(n)$. We characterize the set of weight-5 linear light patterns, and the set of weight-5 linear patterns more generally. Along the way we identify several new infinite classes of linear patterns, which support the Pettie-Tardos conjecture on characterizing all linear light patterns. It was known that there exist infinitely many minimally nonlinear patterns. We identify a specific infinite set of minimally nonlinear patterns. We also prove that there are $2^{Ω(r)}$ weight-$r$ minimally nonlinear patterns, and that every minimally nonlinear pattern has extremal function $O(n\log n)$, with the exception of the 4-cycle. We classify many of the outstanding weight-5 patterns according to their extremal function, leaving only a small set remaining. The newly classified weight-5 patterns have extremal function $Θ(n)$ or $Θ(nα(n))$. We also exhibit a large number of weight-6 patterns with extremal function $Θ(n\log n/\log\log n)$, which is notable in that this function had not been encountered before for any single pattern $P$, though it was known to be the correct extremal function for a pair of forbidden patterns.

papers.title: Gram's law for moving targets of the Riemann zeta-function
papers.abstract: We study the solutions of $ζ(s)=f(s)$ for targets $f$ that grow with $|s|$, and Gram's law for them: the statement that each shifted Gram interval contains exactly one solution. The deviation from Gram's law is an integer phase-slip counter, equal up to rounding to $-\frac{1}{2}S(t;x_c)$, where $S(t;x)=π^{-1}\argζ(x+it)$ and $x_c\approx 1/2+\log|f(it)|/\log t$ is a balance abscissa determined by the target. If $|f|\asymp t^κ$ with $κ>κ_1=0.5339\ldots$, where $\sum_p\arcsin(p^{-1/2-κ_1})=π$, and $\arg f$ converges, then every sufficiently high shifted Gram interval contains exactly one solution, which is simple; this localises the fixed points of $ζ$. The threshold is sharp: for $f=c(-s)^κ$ with $1/2<κ<κ_1$, Gram's law fails in $\asymp T$ intervals up to height $T$, and for $0<κ\le 1/2$ it fails infinitely often but with density zero. In both ranges the counter has an explicit limiting distribution. For targets growing more slowly than any power, such as $\log(-s)$, the solutions lie on average $(1+o(1))\log|f(iT)|/\log T$ to the left of the critical line. If $\log|f(iT)|/\sqrt{\log\log T}\to\infty$, the proportion of solutions to the right of the line tends to $0$, whereas for fixed targets Selberg conjectured a quarter, and the counting error at the shifted Gram points is asymptotically Gaussian with variance $(8π^2)^{-1}\log(\log T/\log|f(iT)|)+O(1)$. For $\log(-s)$ the solutions follow neither $θ(T)/π$ nor the zeros of $ζ$. All results are unconditional; numerical computations for $\log(-s)$ illustrate how slowly they take effect.

papers.title: What Should an LLM Know? Knowledge-Guided Warm Starts for Software Optimization
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) process gigabytes in minutes; human experts work far more slowly. Prior studies that explored combinations of human/AI optimizers ignore this gap. Those studies asked systems or humans to label too many examples (e.g., SynthCore needs over four dozen per trial). Here, we test human and AI knowledge under a budget where evaluation is practical (a few dozen labels or fewer). We compare five baselines (random search, RRP, EZR, few-shot prompting, and a budget-matched SynthCore variant) against three ways to give an LLM domain knowledge before it proposes its first configurations: (1) AMP lists the domain's rules, then checks each candidate against them; (2) HKMA adds scouted data or documentation to the prompt; and (3) H-DKP has human experts correct the LLM's rules. We find that domain knowledge improves the "start-up" phase of LLM optimization, but only when that knowledge is checked, by the LLM itself or by a human expert. Across 49 datasets, unchecked knowledge did no better than few-shot prompting or EZR. On the other hand, AMP's self-checking variant (AMP-4) reached the best statistical rank in 44 of 49 datasets (budget-matched SynthCore: 23 of 49), and H-DKP did so in 7 of 8 expert studies. These checks cost little: half a cent of LLM calls per trial, or 6 to 10 expert contacts. Hence we say LLMs may not need more data, but rather their knowledge needs checking (and checking is cheap).

papers.title: Training for sustainable scientific software in the AI era: from code production to scientific stewardship
papers.abstract: Generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are changing how researchers interact with scientific software. Their effects on productivity vary across tasks and users, but they can weaken the connection between producing a successful computational artifact and retaining scientific command over the consequential choices and evidence on which it depends. For high-energy physics, this shifts part of the training challenge from code production toward scientific stewardship: researchers must be able to validate, explain, reproduce, maintain, and justify software and workflows partly generated or modified by AI. We argue that AI-aware software training should therefore combine dedicated instruction on AI systems with the integration of AI into established software and analysis training. Testing, provenance, reproducibility, resource judgment, and scientific validation should be exercised in AI-assisted workflows, with competence judged by the evidence supporting a result rather than by code generation alone. We frame this as a problem of sustainable scientific software: AI-assisted workflows should remain trustworthy and maintainable, use computational resources responsibly, and avoid making core competence unnecessarily dependent on privileged access to particular tools or infrastructure.

papers.title: A level is not a rank: an empirical audit of quantile-to-index conversion in 10 released conformal-prediction libraries
papers.abstract: Context. A conformal interval at 0.90 keeps that guarantee only at the right rank: a fresh score falls at or below the rth smallest of n with probability r/(n + 1). The libraries we study instead hand a level to a quantile function, which can land elsewhere. At n = 20, the upper end of statsforecast's interval sits at position 18.05 where rank 19 is required. Objective. Where does installed code resolve the wrong rank, at what cost in coverage, and what does it return when no rank reaches the level? Method. We audit 39 sites where a level becomes an index in 10 pinned packages, a named set rather than a systematic search. 12 are classified by running them, 11 through their shared numpy method, the rest from source. Coverage is paired against the required rank on the same scores. Results. All 7 tabular implementations reach the required rank. In darts, on one code path, coverage is unchanged (0.0000) where the ranks agree and 0.0280 to 0.0560 lower where they differ; a second archive repeats that split but not its range. Below the feasibility floor, $n < 1/α- 1$, of 14 public call paths 5 silently return a finite number; the rest raise or warn. Conclusions. Quantile interfaces take only a level; statsforecast's default calibrates below its floor. 6 of 19 upstream filings have merged, one fixing a coverage shortfall. A conformance suite classifies helpers by the rank they reach, and a checklist guides review.

papers.title: Computing with Orientation-Dependent Vector Fields in Crystallographic Texture Analysis
papers.abstract: We present a computational framework for representing orientation-dependent vector fields. Building on (arXiv:2608.21235), we translate the differential-geometric formulation into crystallographic notation and focus on its computational use in crystallographic texture analysis. In crystallographic applications, small orientation changes are commonly described by rotation vectors, spin tensors, or infinitesimal misorientations. By contrast, vector fields in harmonic computations are usually represented by components with respect to Euler-angle derivatives, following the classical formulation of generalized spherical harmonics. This representation is convenient but numerically unfavorable. We instead use rotation-vector components, extending a familiar description of individual orientation changes to orientation-dependent vector fields. In this representation, vector fields are described by three scalar component functions, which can be expanded into generalized spherical harmonics. We derive frequency-domain formulas for gradient, divergence, and curl, enabling their evaluation directly on harmonic coefficients. In particular, the gradient of a band-limited scalar function remains band-limited with the same bandwidth.

papers.title: Numerical approximation of Benjamin-Ono type models for two-dimensional internal waves
papers.abstract: In this paper we analyze the numerical approximation with spectral methods of two asymptotic models for the two-dimensional propagation of internal waves in a two-layer system of fluids with rigid-lid condition. The semidiscretization in space of the periodic initial-value problem with the spectral Fourier-Galerkin method is introduced and some error estimates are derived. Then the semidiscrete system is integrated in time with the Implicit Midpoint Rule and several numerical experiments illustrate the performance of the corresponding full discretization.

papers.title: Sharp error estimates for Lagrange interpolation and Kantorovich-type operators in weighted $L_p$-spaces
papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish sharp direct and inverse approximation estimates for algebraic Lagrange interpolation polynomials and Kantorovich-type operators in weighted $L_p$ spaces on $[-1,1]$. A well-known limitation in the theory of approximation by interpolation polynomials states that for small rates of convergence $α\le 1/p$, classical moduli of smoothness fail to provide matching direct and inverse estimates due to the insufficiency of integral metrics to determine pointwise values at the interpolation nodes. To overcome this difficulty, we introduce new special semi-discrete measures of smoothness based on Steklov averaging operators, which combine global $L_p$-smoothness with discrete deviations from Steklov averages at the interpolation nodes. By using these measures, we establish fully matching direct and inverse approximation theorems for Lagrange interpolation polynomials, thereby providing complete two-sided characterizations of the rate of convergence for an arbitrary rate $α> 0$. As a natural application of the developed approach, we also obtain corresponding direct and inverse estimates, as well as strong converse inequalities, for Kantorovich-type operators constructed via Lagrange polynomials.

papers.title: Reflections on Thiele, Schur, and Continued Fractions
papers.abstract: We survey several classical continued-fraction constructions from a common point of view centered on linear-fractional transformations, interpolation, and the recurrence relations they generate. Beginning with Thiele's interpolation algorithm, we trace how similar mechanisms reappear in the Schur algorithm, Wall's continued fractions, and multipoint Nevanlinna--Pick interpolation. Particular attention is paid to the emergence of $R_{II}$-type continued fractions, which arise naturally as even parts of Thiele continued fractions, and to the associated pencils of tridiagonal matrices. A detour through Euler's continued-fraction formula illustrates how rational Nevanlinna functions lead naturally to finite $R_{II}$-pencils, while the Schur algorithm is related to Wall pencils and, through a different reorganization, to CMV matrices. We also discuss a modified Schur transformation that removes an interpolation condition at a pair of symmetric points, which leads to a linear pencil of two Hermitian tridiagonal matrices. Finally, we indicate how periodically occurring interpolation nodes at infinity convert $R_{II}$-pencils into ordinary banded matrices, suggesting a connection with GMP matrices.

papers.title: A Differential Theory of Quality-Resource Trade-offs for AI Model Selection: The Multiresource Frontier and Its Minimax Price
papers.abstract: Comparing AI models across resource budgets yields quality-resource frontiers relating error to latency, parameter count, training compute, and energy. Offset power laws summarize such frontiers, but their fitted parameters reveal neither the price-independent geometry nor the manner in which trade-offs extend across several resource channels. This paper addresses both gaps by developing a differential theory in which this structure is made explicit. Each frontier admits a price-independent plane-curve representation relating the effective number of active resource channels, $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = s^2/κ$ (squared slope over curvature), to the remaining log-error depth, $ΔS = \ln(\varepsilon/\varepsilon_{\infty})$. This representation separates intrinsic shape from the scale and origin of the resource axis. Complete monotonicity and divisibility yield differential inequalities and frontier bounds. When each of $N$ resources contributes one active channel, the theory gives the parameter-free operating rule $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1$ in delivered units and derives minimax resource prices $λ^{\star}_i = α_i/(N+1)$ with an exact worst-case regret of $\ln(N+1)$ nats. The results make it possible to interpret measured frontiers and compare resource costs without hand-chosen exchange rates. The theory is evaluated on 117 published frontiers and implemented in the open-source package nn-rank, which derives prices from measured quality and cost, ranks candidates, and reports supported choices and minimax regret: https://github.com/ABrain-One/nn-rank

papers.title: HydroMind: A Checkable Agent for Autonomous Hydrological Research
papers.abstract: General-purpose coding agents have written code for hydrological and Earth-system models. In these studies the researchers decided in advance how the model would be evaluated, for example the test period, the scoring function, and the standard the model had to meet. No study has tested what happens when the agent makes these decisions itself: how many of its claims are supported by its own data, code, and results, and whether readers can check them. Both may depend on the agent's harness, that is, the tools it can call and the written instructions it follows. We compared three harnesses: the agent's own harness; this harness plus the modeling tools of HydroMind, a hydrological modeling system we developed for general-purpose agents, which run every model through fixed commands and store its settings, trained model, and predictions; and both plus HydroMind's research procedure, under which the agent writes a research design before running any model and records every change to it. Under each harness, the same agent studied four open questions in hydrological model development and was given only the data. Under the three harnesses, the experiments submitted 23, 20, and 41 claims, each stating that one model or approach is better than, worse than, or similar to another. A claim does not hold if the difference recomputed from the experiment's own code and predictions disagrees with it, or if the code did not compare the two models or approaches the claim names. Under the three harnesses, 30%, 20%, and 5% of the claims did not hold. A statistical test, confidence interval, or decision rule that lets readers judge the stated difference was reported for 48%, 53%, and 83% of the claims. With the language model unchanged, changing only the harness reduced the share of claims that do not hold and increased the share that readers can check.

papers.title: Human-AI Mutualism Is Unstable under Capability Asymmetry
papers.abstract: One hope for a good human future alongside advanced AI rests on enduring mutualism: humans and AI will need each other, so the relationship will stay good for both. We argue that this hope fails as AI capability grows. Bargaining guarantees each side only what it would get if bargaining failed. For humans, this can be less than they had before AI. In a simple game-theoretic model, humans stay as well off as before AI without alignment only while they have leverage over the AI: either the AI depends on what they supply, or they can impose costs on the AI that are large relative to what the AI can produce. Once humans have neither kind of leverage, they stay as well off as before AI only if the AI is aligned with them. If the AI's goals are insatiable, the alignment required approaches perfect alignment as AI capability grows. Thus, mutualism is not a substitute for alignment. And when AI variants that keep more resources spread faster, alignment lasts only while misaligned variants are reliably sanctioned. In these two senses, human-AI mutualism is unstable.

papers.title: Error Analysis of Deep Learning
papers.abstract: This review examines deep learning theory through the lens of error decomposition, systematically addressing approximation, statistical, and optimization errors. We trace the development of error analyses from bounds on individual error components to frameworks that account for all three. Using nonparametric regression and the Deep Ritz Method as dual running examples, we demonstrate how these analyses apply across fundamentally different loss structures. We then review representative analyses in scientific machine learning, generative learning, reinforcement learning, representation learning, and large language models, showing how learning errors affect solutions, distributions, and predictions through problem-specific arguments. Throughout, we clarify which error components are controlled, how they are combined, and what assumptions are needed to obtain guarantees for trained networks.

papers.title: Does a label survive the loop? A screen of necessary physical conditions for a self-measuring system, with a pre-registered test on fly connectomes
papers.abstract: Theories that tie experience to a system that re-reads its own state rarely say what a physical substrate must supply for such a loop to run. We state necessary conditions as measurable bounds in one currency: the number of rounds, each one write, hold and re-read, that a written label survives.A floor follows from fundamental constants. Tier 1 asks whether a carrier can hold the label; it is the published quality-factor screen, restated in rounds and extended to a population code. Tier 2 bounds how many rounds a quantum resource survives in a loop that keeps a record. Tier 3 asks whether a network contains a compartment, a set of neurons that a random walk leaves more slowly than it mixes inside. Tier 4 compares what the loop and an outside observer can recover. We implement Tiers 3 and 4 on three connectomes of Drosophila. Exploration of two animals singled out the heading system of the ellipsoid body. Five criteria were then registered and run once on a third animal, and all were met with all connections counted. One was met narrowly, and two fail in that data set when connections of one or two synapses are removed, which we trace in part to synapse detection. As a population code the heading label holds about two bits for seven seconds. The screen can exclude substrates. Passing it is not evidence of experience.

papers.title: Reusing formal Vlasov-Maxwell proofs to certify plasma solver outputs
papers.abstract: AI now produces machine-checked mathematics faster than researchers can read it. Can such theorems do practical computational work?
