A magnitude-based temporal rule assigns guidance reuse to low-magnitude blocks and reserves fresh guidance for the remaining blocks, with a single integer controlling the computation budget. The resulting schedule requires no additional router training or per-budget threshold search. Evaluated on CogVideoX-2B with 4,720 videos per configuration across all sixteen official VBench dimensions, BATMoS achieves the highest total score among the eight allocation policies and comes within 0.10 points of full classifier-free guidance using 20\% fewer branch evaluations. BATMoS also composes with feature reuse, reducing computation from 80 to 62 effective branch evaluations with a 0.11-point decrease in total score. These findings make temporal guidance allocation a practical mechanism for extracting more generation quality from a fixed inference budget.

papers.title: GauntletScore: Auditable Fact-Checking That Matches the Best Published Checkers on LLM-AggreFact
papers.abstract: Checking whether a generated sentence is supported by its source document is a standard safeguard for AI-written text, and the strongest published checkers are single models. We describe GauntletScore, an evidence engine whose few rules and thresholds were set on the benchmark's development split. It puts typed questions to independent readers from different providers and records each answer as a measurement in an evidence ledger. It combines the measurements with a fixed Bayesian rule that counts a contradiction only when two readers agree. On the full LLM-AggreFact test split (29,320 claims across 11 datasets), following the leaderboard's approach, GauntletScore achieves 79.51 balanced accuracy, above every average published on the leaderboard as of 15 November 2026. That places it level with the best of them, nimble-v4-max (79.45 from its published dataset scores; the engine's 95% interval, 78.47 to 80.53, contains it). On the same claims it beats two of its three readers used alone (Readers A and B) by 1.66 and 2.17 points (95% intervals 0.80 to 2.53 and 1.29 to 3.06). Without AggreFact-CNN, described below, the leads are 0.90 and 1.32 and both intervals stay above zero. The engine also records the evidence behind every verdict, which a single model does not. Its largest margin is on full-length news articles checked against multi-sentence summaries (AggreFact-CNN), a format that resembles much regulated writing. There it scores 76.45, the best on the leaderboard, against 70.1 for the next best and 63.9 to 67.8 for the six systems with the highest averages. The test split was run once, on an engine frozen before the first test claim, under a stopping plan committed in advance. We release per-claim predictions and the scoring script.

papers.title: New necessary conditions on $h$-vectors of simplicial balls
papers.abstract: Although the $h$-vectors of simplicial balls of dimension at most $4$ have been completely characterized, much less is known in dimensions $5$ and higher. We establish new necessary conditions on the $h$-vectors of simplicial balls in these dimensions. Together with the necessary conditions of Billera and Lee and the sufficient conditions of Kolins, our results yield a complete characterization of the $h$-vectors of $5$- and $6$-dimensional simplicial balls. We also give a characterization of $h$-vectors of simplicial balls of any dimension with neighborly boundary.

papers.title: Causal Input--Output Modeling with Prior Information
papers.abstract: We study the problem of inferring a causal input--output model from unpaired marginal observations and a given prior coupling. We formulate this problem using entropic causal optimal transport, which seeks a coupling that preserves the observed marginals, satisfies a one--sided causality constraint, and remains close to the prior. For Gaussian marginals and general quadratic costs, we prove that the optimal coupling is Gaussian and reduce the problem to a finite--dimensional optimization over covariance matrices. Using a Cholesky transformation to simplify the causality constraint, we derive a Lagrangian dual formulation and develop a block coordinate descent algorithm with explicit update formulas. We establish linear convergence of the algorithm, with explicit convergence rates, and prove stability of the optimal coupling under marginal covariance perturbations and derive a statistical error bound. We further show its equivalence to Sinkhorn iterations. Numerical experiments demonstrate the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithm and illustrate the predictive advantages of causal couplings.

papers.title: An AI-Based OSSE Framework to Evaluate Learned Physical Consistency: A Multi-Model Study Using FourCastNet, Aurora, Prithvi WxC, and GraphCast
papers.abstract: Observing System Simulation Experiments (OSSEs) are a central methodology for evaluating future atmospheric observing systems. We present the first AI-based OSSE framework to test whether different AI weather models can reproduce comparable physical impact from new observations that traditional physics based models generate. We evaluate four distinct architectural AI models on the Charney conjecture that incomplete historical observations can infer the present state of the atmospheric. We considner- FourCastNet V2, GraphCast, Aurora and Prithvi WxC and integrate each autoregressively over a 60-day forecast horizon. After a 30-day spin-up, we insert ERA5 temperature fields to infer winds and related atmospheric fields. Similar OSSE experiments are conducted for wind insertion. We measure the performance of each model's response to observational information on a 30-day data assimilation cycle forecast with and without data insertion. Distinct architectural AI weather models respond differently to the same OSSE observations. Foundation models (i.e. Prithvi WxC and Aurora), produce the strongest impact. For example, while GraphCast is the weakest, all three of the four models capture the temperature-to-geopotential height response. The two foundational models retain a positive, non-trivial, tropical zonal wind at 500 hPa response to temperature insertion. Various data insertion experiments can vary significantly even within a given architecture. We identify an architecture-specific numerical instability in GraphCast's full 37-level configuration that produces a runaway feedback concentrated at the uppermost levels with ERA5 temperature insertion correctable by excluding levels at or below 100 hPa.

papers.title: Single-Vertex Metropolis on Minor-Free Graphs: A General EPTAS
papers.abstract: We consider a class of combinatorial optimization problems where the goal is to find a largest induced subgraph with a prescribed property. We assume that the property is preserved by taking induced subgraphs and disjoint unions, holds for all edgeless graphs, and can be tested in polynomial time. We study the single-vertex Metropolis process for this class of problems. We show that on graphs excluding an arbitrary fixed minor $H$, this process is a randomized efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme. Starting from any feasible solution on a graph with $n$ vertices, it finds a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation within $\exp(O_H(\varepsilon^{-2})) n(n+\log(1/δ))$ steps with probability at least $1-δ$. This includes maximum independent set, maximum induced forest, maximum induced bipartite subgraph, and maximum induced subgraph of degree at most one. The proof uses improving exchanges on one fixed division of the input graph into regions. A recursive separator construction performs each exchange inside a region of size $r$ in at most $2r$ moves, with temporary loss $O_H(\sqrt r)$. We count move sequences through each transition and bound the probability of avoiding all near-optimal states. The general theorem bounds the number of Metropolis steps in terms of the temporary loss along improvement paths. We extend the result to bounded weight imbalance and give a weighted-star obstruction for unrestricted weights.

papers.title: A mechanistic characterization of missingness at random
papers.abstract: The missingness-at-random (MAR) assumption underlying many missing-data methods describes abstract statistical independences, whereas practitioners reason more naturally about the causal mechanisms that generate missingness. To bridge this gap, we provide a mechanistic characterization of MAR in terms of paths in a directed acyclic graph (DAG) modified to allow certain edges to cease to operate when an incomplete variable is missing, a property termed "context-specific causal irrelevance (CSCI)". Under a faithfulness condition, MAR holds if and only if the modified DAG contains no MAR-violating paths. Without CSCI, this condition reduces to a previously established d-separation condition, VMAR; thus, MAR without VMAR requires specific kinds of CSCI, as can occur with monotone dropout. These results shift the burden on investigators from passively invoking MAR to justifying, on substantive grounds, the specific mechanisms it requires. We then consider identification of a target law p(v) of variables V by a MAR-assuming analysis, e.g., multiple imputation, that includes complete auxiliary variables Z (variables not in V). Barring a perfect cancellation, such an analysis recovers p(v) if and only if MAR holds with respect to V and Z jointly. We show that if there exists any set of auxiliaries such that (V, Z) obeys MAR, then the complete candidate auxiliaries that are ancestors of the target variables or their missingness indicators form a sufficient set. Contrary to standard recommendations, not all candidate auxiliaries should be used: even complete auxiliaries can introduce MAR violations that would not otherwise occur. We illustrate these results with simulations and an analysis of sexual identity change in the Stockholm Public Health Cohort, where our results indicate that a candidate auxiliary, income, should be excluded; including it attenuated estimates toward the null.

papers.title: Perfect matching complexes of antiprism graphs and independence complexes of generalized Petersen graphs $GP(n,2)$
papers.abstract: We show that the perfect matching complexes of antiprism graphs and the independence complexes of the generalized Petersen graphs $GP(n, 2)$ are homotopy equivalent to wedges of spheres, and we determine the number and dimensions of the spheres. For the former we compute the initial values of Adamaszek's recursion for the independence complexes of cubes of cycles.

papers.title: Frame Based Inelasticity for Strength and Fracture in Anisotropic Media
papers.abstract: A field theory is presented for predicting damage and fracture in brittle materials. Four concepts are used: a new nonlocal deformation gradient for dynamic stress analysis in anisotropic media, a new type of phase field coming from a constitutive law, the evolution of material displacement from Newton's second law, and a new incorporation of scaled strength surfaces into constitutive laws for predicting dynamic and quasi-static fracture patterns. The elastic softening is governed by the strain dynamics through the constitutive law and in this way we provide the two way coupling between strain and fracture. Simulations validating the approach for both dynamic and quasi-static fracture analysis are compared to experimental results and other simulation methods. The model is capable of predicting material strength in titania and the competition between strength and energy in soda lime glass and titana and captures dynamic crack branching in soda lime glass and concrete.

papers.title: Computed Permutation Trellis Coding: Near-Optimal Quantization from Two Multiplications and a 64-Byte Table
papers.abstract: We propose Computed Permutation Trellis Coding (CPTC), a low-bit quantization format for tensors written once and read many times. Formats that round each value on its own, such as INT4 and FP4, waste a large part of their bits against the information-theoretic ideal. Trellis codes recover this loss by encoding values jointly, but prior decoders either need a large lookup table for their best quality or compute values with a hash that restricts what they can decode. CPTC's decoder multiplies its state by two coefficients and adds the top bits of the products to index a 64-byte table. Because that sum is not uniformly distributed, the rarely used ends of a small table can hold values far out in the tails. One decoder serves every bit width from 1 to 6, reproduces the standard integer and floating-point formats exactly, and comes within 0.07 bits of the ideal at 4 bits. It matches a random-permutation trellis code whose table is thousands of times larger, and exceeds every QTIP codebook. In LLM weight quantization without fine-tuning, CPTC has the lowest KL divergence to the unquantized model at every tested bit width on Llama 3.1 8B and 70B Instruct against QTIP's codebooks (by up to 27%). The decoder has been built into the AWS Trainium 4 AI accelerator, where it runs at the throughput of the native FP4 and FP8 formats for a negligible fraction of the systolic array's area. Fused encoding kernels quantize an 8B model's linear layers in under two minutes on one GPU and, in cycle-level simulation, on one Trainium 4 chip.

papers.title: Structural functional identifiability of unknown differential equation observation maps
papers.abstract: In many differential equation models of real-world systems, the mechanistic structure of the dynamics is known, but the map from the dynamics to the observations is not. This is potentially problematic, as it can prevent us from e.g. learning model parameter values from data. Examples where this occurs include measuring a fluorescent marker as a proxy for the dynamics of a cellular circuit, and using wastewater measurements to follow the development of an epidemic. The nascent field of hybrid modelling, in which machine learning components (like neural networks) are embedded within mechanistic models, provides the tools to learn such maps. Here, the system's dynamics keep their mechanistic form, while a neural network represents the unknown observation map and is trained alongside any unknown core system parameters. This raises a question of identifiability: when can the true observation map be learnt, and when does one simply learn some map that transforms the dynamics into the available data? Building on previous work, we show how structural functional identifiability analysis can establish whether a model's unknown observation maps and core system parameters are identifiable, i.e. can be uniquely learnt from data. We both prove general results on when models with unknown observation maps are, and are not, identifiable, and demonstrate a general methodology (based on differential algebra) for assessing the identifiability of such models. This paves the way for applying classic differential equation workflows to the many real-world systems that contain such unknown maps.

papers.title: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory
papers.abstract: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, currently in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.

papers.title: An Explainable Agentic AI Framework for Distribution System Load Restoration
papers.abstract: Distribution system load restoration is a sequential decision-making problem in which restoration actions must maximize served load, prioritize critical loads, and preserve power-flow feasibility. This paper proposes an explainable agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for distribution system load restoration. The proposed framework uses multiple large language model (LLM) agents for planner guidance, strategic plan generation, decision arbitration, memory-based feedback, and explanation generation. Unlike unconstrained LLM-based control, the proposed method restricts agent decisions to feasible restoration actions and evaluates all candidate plans using deterministic AC power-flow feasibility checks. The framework is evaluated on IEEE 33-bus and 69-bus distribution feeders, as well as a larger IEEE 118-bus test case, and compared against reinforcement learning and planning baselines. The results show that the proposed agentic framework achieves better restoration performance while producing structured explanations for operator-facing decision support. A direct comparison with a Single-LLM-Agent baseline further shows that the proposed multi-agent decomposition improves weighted restored load and critical-load recovery compared with a monolithic LLM decision structure.

papers.title: Theoretical Instability Models of Quasi-Periodic Eruptions
papers.abstract: The nature of the Quasi-Periodic Eruptions (QPE) is still not firmly established while the phenomenon probes the innermost part of the accretion flow undergoing dramatic changes. In this chapter we review the possibility that the observed rapid variability is caused by the accretion disk instability. We summarise the defining observational properties of QPE sources: time scales of recurrence, the amplitudes of soft X-ray flares, high coherence over many cycles, and comparatively modest time-averaged luminosities. We then translate these into constraints on the characteristic radius, accretion rate, and energy reservoir of the inner disk. We review the main classes of disk instabilities relevant to supermassive black holes: radiation pressure induced thermal/viscous limit cycles, magnetically mediated inner disk transitions, and coupling to disk winds that can produce the oscillatory behavior. For each scenario we discuss the required parameter space (black hole mass, Eddington ratio, viscosity prescription, and truncation radius), the predicted spectral and timing signatures, and the degree of fine tuning needed to reproduce the observed duty cycles and flare morphologies. We highlight key tensions, including the extremely soft spectra, short recurrence times compared with standard viscous times at tens of gravitational radii, and the weak or absent contemporaneous optical/UV variability in several systems. Finally, we outline observational tests that may help distinguish between instability driven and geometrical or orbital models: phase resolved spectroscopy to track the temperature evolution, searches for hysteresis in hardness-intensity diagrams, reverberation and absorption variability tied to winds, and long baseline monitoring to measure drift in period and energy output.

papers.title: Weight-Space Programming for Materials Science
papers.abstract: A materials discovery campaign often begins with almost no measurements of the property it is searching for, and the models that rank candidates or screen the output of a generator then have to be built from those first few labels. Following recent work on weight-space programming, in which a language model writes the weights of a small network directly as text, we show that a general-purpose model, given the task in words, the names of the inputs and a network of 16 hidden units with every weight set to zero, can provide this starting point by filling in all of the weights from what it has learned about materials. With no labels, the networks of the strongest model rank experimental alloys at Spearman co-efficient = 0.64 to 0.79, where the best of five simple descriptors reaches 0.47 to 0.62. They rank the bulk modulus of crystals added during generative discovery loops at 0.95, where the inverse volume per atom reaches 0.89, and 35 phase-equilibrium targets computed with Thermo-Calc at a mean of 0.67, close to the 0.70 of an extrapolation from calculated binary and ternary data. As the prior mean of a Gaussian process they raise the ranking at five labels from 0.35 to 0.69 on alloys and from 0.15 to 0.95 on crystals, and they lower the regret of Bayesian optimization significantly on 4 of 5 experimental tasks and on 13 to 16 of 33 computed targets, depending on how multiple tests are corrected, without raising it significantly on any. The same networks also serve as the mean of a Bayesian neural network and as a screen for the samples of two crystal generators, where they do as well as standard models trained on 400 labeled structures. The gain is confined to the first tens of labels and to targets that no rule or sub-system extrapolation already ranks.

papers.title: PS-HalluBench: Taxonomy-Driven Benchmarking of LLM Hallucinations in Power Systems
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for power-system applications, yet their reliability in engineering analysis remains uncertain. We introduce PS-HalluBench, a manually constructed benchmark of 200 questions that evaluates hallucination-related failures across five power-system task categories: numerical reasoning, network topology, constraint verification, false-premise acceptance, and abstention. We evaluate ten LLMs over the benchmark, yielding 39.35\% overall correctness, with constraint verification achieving only 21.75\%, and highlighting persistent difficulties in engineering reasoning. We further investigate engineering-grounded reasoning through numerical solver support and verified network information both of which show significant performance improvement. The findings reveal important limitations of standalone LLM reasoning and motivate integrating LLMs with verified engineering tools for reliable power-system analysis.

papers.title: Locally Linear Generalized Single Index Regression
papers.abstract: In this work we propose and analyze a procedure for estimating a generalized single-index regression model. This generalized single-index regression framework models the conditional mean of the responses $Y$ as a function of the covariates $X$ where the mapping is assumed to have the form $f \circ g$, where $g$ is $β$-Hölder with $β\geq 2$ and $f$ can be a discontinuous function of bounded variation. We propose a general procedure that operates under minimal assumptions about the distribution of covariates $X$, requiring only boundedness, sufficient smoothness and absolute continuity with respect to Lebesgue. Our procedure jointly estimates the gradient vector $\hat v(x) \approx \nabla g(x)$ and the conditional mean $μ(x) = f(g(x))$ by solving a localized weighted linear least squares problem. We derive central limit theorems for gradient vector estimates $\hat{v}_x$ and regression estimates $\hatμ(x)$, and we derive rates of convergence for our approach, illustrating that it indeed achieves a stochastic convergence rate matching the minimax mean squared error rate when $β= 2$ and $f$ has a locally Lipschitz derivative. Unlike prior approaches our velocity estimation results accommodate link functions in the local bounded-variation class, allowing for nonsmooth and even discontinuous links while retaining consistency and asymptotic normality at almost every inference point. Finally, we instantiate this model in the situation where $g = Π$ is a closest point projection onto a compact and regular embedded $C^3$ curve $γ$, a setting recently studied in the literature. We also supplement our theoretical results with experiments on real and synthetic data to demonstrate the utility of our procedure.

papers.title: On Formal Counterfactual Explanations
papers.abstract: Counterfactual explanations are often seen as counterfactual conditionals under closest-world semantics, requiring one to reason over all minimally distant counterexamples. In contrast, formal XAI typically relies on feature-based abductive explanations (AXps) and contrastive explanations (CXps), which admit efficient computation and a minimal hitting-set duality. This paper bridges these perspectives by (i) characterizing closest-world counterfactual explanations explicitly as a disjunctive normal form over all minimally distant counterexample instances, and (ii) introducing conjunctive counterfactual explanations (CFXps), a subclass of counterfactual antecedents restricted to conjunctions of feature literals that guarantee prediction change. The paper establishes structural results connecting CXps, AXps and CFXps: every CXp induces an AXp for its witness instance, and every CXp together with a witness AXp induces a CFXp whose support is precisely determined by that AXp. These theoretical results yield a modular approach for computing CFXps using existing AXp/CXp machinery. Experiments on a representative set of benchmarks using tree ensembles and neural networks show that CFXp extraction is practically efficient. Compared with popular point-based counterfactual explainers, CFXps generally require no more feature changes and can guarantee the counterfactual prediction beyond a single instance.

papers.title: DiagTrace: An Interactive Benchmark for Clinical Decision Making
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on medical question answering and diagnostic reasoning benchmarks. However, existing evaluations typically provide all patient information upfront and assess only the final diagnosis or rationale. This setup ignores the need to acquire diagnostic evidence incrementally from incomplete information in real-world diagnosis. To bridge this gap, we introduce DiagTrace, a source-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can reconstruct the documented diagnostic trajectory through interactive information seeking. Each benchmark instance is built from a PubMed Central case report and includes an initial presentation, an event bank, a clinical course, and diagnostic references. DiagTrace contains 510 cases across eight specialties, with 225 used to evaluate four LLMs on clinical-course alignment, interaction quality, and efficiency. Results reveal trade-offs in coverage, source-consistent ordering, and turn use.

papers.title: Stokes flow in a wedge with a moving contact point: well-posedness with a fixed contact angle and Navier slip
papers.abstract: We study 2D Stokes flow in a wedge-like region bounded by a solid substrate with Navier slip and by a free surface driven by surface tension. The two meet at a moving contact point with a fixed contact angle. This is the model of a moving contact line at scales below the slip length, in its simplest setting. The slip length is the only length scale, and nothing is prescribed at the contact point beyond the angle: no relaxation law for the angle, and no contact-point dissipation. Slip removes the paradox found by Huh and Scriven, the infinite dissipation at a contact line that moves without slip, but in this model a weaker singularity remains. We give, to our knowledge, the first rigorous characterisation of this singularity for solutions of the free-boundary problem near the stationary state. For small contact angles and small initial data satisfying two compatibility conditions, we prove local existence, uniqueness and Lipschitz dependence on the data. The compatibility conditions are the price of the fixed angle for solutions regular in time up to the initial time. Rather than hiding the singularity, the solution class carries it explicitly in corner expansions. The velocity is continuous up to the contact point. The pressure has a logarithmic singularity, the slip-regularised version of that of Huh and Scriven. Its coefficient is proportional to the contact-point velocity. The slope of the free boundary has a corresponding logarithmic correction, the slip-scale counterpart of the Cox-Voinov relation. The linearised problem combines terms of different scaling, which prevents a direct treatment by the Mellin transform. We solve it by a Lax-Milgram argument, and an auxiliary test function problem shows that the variational solution satisfies the equations. Explicit Mellin representations then yield the corner expansions, and the nonlinear problem is solved by a contraction argument.

papers.title: The interplay between ionized and warm molecular gas in the turbulent intragroup medium of Stephan's Quintet
papers.abstract: Using JWST MIRI spectroscopy, we explore the multi-phase intergalactic gas in the hot halo of the Stephan's Quintet compact group. Unlike the coolest H2 emission, which commonly shows double- peaked profiles corresponding to the velocity of the intruder and the intragroup gas, the ionized Neon emission-lines are often systematically shifted redwards in radial velocity away from the lowest H2 peak, and into the region corresponding to gas decelerated by the collision of the intruder galaxy with intragroup gas. The majority of the brightest clumps of ionized gas are spatially correlated with the brightest H2 clumps, suggesting they are coherent structures caught up in the opposing gas flows. Gas that is progressively heated, is shifted in velocity further from the velocity of the coldest H2 peaks. Larger and larger shifts in velocity are seen as one progresses from cool to warm molecular hydrogen, to lower-excitation (Neon lines) ionized and strongly shocked heated ionized gas (gas-phase Iron). The majority of the ionized Neon in the intergalactic medium is consistent with excitation in low-velocity shocks. We suggest that this behavior is the result of gas of progressively lower densities being shocked and accelerated by the interaction of pre-existing clouds with a hot flow created by the blast-wave from the collision between the intruder and the intragroup gas. One exception is the extragalactic star forming region, SQ-A, which shows higher-excitation ionized emission lines consistent with heating from a young starburst, consistent with previous photometry of young star clusters in the region.

papers.title: Supporting Researcher Control in AI-Assisted Social Media Analysis: A Mixed-Methods Study of AI4OSN
papers.abstract: High-quality annotated datasets are critical for advancing computational social science (CSS) research, yet collecting, curating, and analyzing large-scale data from dynamic sources such as online social networks (OSNs) remains a persistent bottleneck. Researchers must also translate substantive questions into queries, relevance criteria, and defensible interpretations. Large language models (LLMs) can assist, but they can also obscure the judgments, potentially reducing researcher oversight and critical evaluation. We present AI4OSN, a mixed-initiative platform that keeps researchers in control of data collection, relevance labeling, and sensemaking while making AI assistance available as an inspectable advisory resource. In a systematic user study (N=18) using X/Twitter data, participants reported above-benchmark perceived usability (mean SUS score of 79.7), increased confidence in LLM-assisted annotation and analysis tasks, and low cognitive workload during AI-supported sensemaking. Notably, novice participants showed descriptively greater alignment and higher reported agreement with AI output than experienced participants, underscoring the need to support differentiated verification practices across expertise levels. Overall, this work contributes both a human-centered system for social data analysis and empirical insights into how AI-assisted interfaces shape researcher behavior, trust, and decision-making. Our findings highlight design opportunities and tensions in building accessible, transparent, and agentic AI systems for social media and web research.

papers.title: Where Should the Lamp Go? Ambient-Aware Lamp Placement for Portraits
papers.abstract: Portraits shape first impressions, and lighting is an important factor. Prior work, such as lighting estimation and portrait relighting, edits lighting after capture but does not guide where to place a light before the shot. This leaves an open question: where should a light go to best light a face? Therefore, we propose LightMatch, a preference-grounded inverse lighting framework that disentangles the controllable light from ambient illumination and optimizes its placement. We first learn a Bradley-Terry quality model from pairwise human judgments. A perception head then regresses spherical-harmonic lighting from frozen self-supervised features via cross-attention. Finally, a placement solver isolates the light via spherical-harmonic linearity and optimizes its reachable position. On held-out environments, LightMatch attains 87.8% of the oracle improvement, outperforming the conventional solver that ignores ambient light by a relative 28.4% and the same pipeline with the widely used DPR estimator by a relative 70.5%. It reaches 73.2% on real OLAT faces of unseen identities and, on our real captures, cuts lamp-direction error by 37.7%.

papers.title: VLA Observations of the Ionized Jet IRAS 16562-3959
papers.abstract: We present new high-resolution, high-sensitivity Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (VLA) A-configuration observations of the high-mass protostellar jet system IRAS 16562-3959 at 3.1 and 6.1 GHz. Our images resolve the five previously known jet components (OE, IE, C, IW, OW) into 21 distinct knots and sub-components, and reveal a new off-axis source, MW. Based on the dynamical timescales from previous works ($τ_{jet} \approx 620$ yr), the spacing and structure of the knots suggest episodic accretion with a mean interval between ejections of $\sim$32 yr. We find that source MW has a substantial increase in peak brightness relative to its marginal detections in previous observations. MW exhibits a spectral index of $α\approx -0.7$, characteristic of synchrotron emission from shock-accelerated relativistic electrons. Equipartition analysis yields a minimum-energy magnetic field strength $B_{me} \approx 0.4$ mG, and a minimum total energy $E_{me} \approx 4.4 \times 10^{42}$ erg. Archival 2MASS Ks data imply a total outflow dynamical age of $\sim$1400 yr, and together with a HST [FeII] 1.64 $μ$m map, the NIR data indicate that the fast jet is embedded in a wide-angle wind with a $\sim 36^\circ$ opening angle.

papers.title: Finite-Time Blow-up for the Radial Mass-Critical Fractional Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation
papers.abstract: We prove that radial negative-energy strong solutions to the focusing mass-critical fractional nonlinear Schrödinger equation \[ i\partial_tu=(-Δ)^su-|u|^{4s/N}u, \quad N\ge2,\quad \frac12<s<1, \] blow up in finite time. This resolves the finite-time blow-up versus infinite-time grow-up alternative left open by Boulenger, Himmelsbach and Lenzmann in the mass-critical regime. The argument uses an exponentially localized virial field together with a dyadic resolvent estimate that transfers the resulting weighted Balakrishnan energy to localized fractional Sobolev norms. When $s\ge N/(2N-1)$, we extend the conclusion to radial $H^s$ solutions by establishing the integrated virial identity at energy regularity. As a consequence, mass-critical ground-state standing waves are strongly unstable by finite-time blow-up.

papers.title: Multiplicity of Solutions for a Class of Logistic Problems
papers.abstract: The present paper investigates the existence and multiplicity of positive solutions to a class of degenerate logistic problems by combining the Nehari manifold {method} with nonlinear generalized Rayleigh quotients. The quotient associated with the Nehari constraint determines the threshold $λ_*$ at which the fibering structure and the Nehari manifold geometry emerge, while a second quotient identifies the zero-energy threshold $λ^*$ associated with the minimizing solution. Together with the threshold $\barλ$ for the existence of nontrivial solutions, these results yield the strict ordering \( 0<λ_*<\barλ<λ^*<λ_1(Ω)<λ_1(Ω_0), \) showing that the Nehari geometry becomes available before nontrivial solutions {exist} and that the zero-energy transition occurs only afterwards. In the variational range, we obtain a positive minimizing solution on $\mathcal N_λ^+$ and a second positive solution via the Mountain Pass Theorem. Complementary sub-supersolution and truncation arguments extend the multiplicity result to the remaining parameter range. We also establish the sign change of the minimizing energy, the blow-up and normalized asymptotic profile of the minimizing solutions as $λ\uparrowλ_1(Ω_0)$, and the convergence of the mountain-pass level $c_λ^m$ to zero as $λ\uparrowλ_1(Ω)$.

papers.title: DreamFAR: Real-Time and Long-Horizon Interaction with Diverse Objects
papers.abstract: World models have shown great potential in serving as a simulator for robot manipulation. However, existing models are either fit to a single environment or lack ability to simulate long-horizon contact-rich events. We present DreamFAR, a world model whose dynamics model is trained from scratch on a large robot-native teleoperation dataset, with no internet-video pretraining. We present an architecture and learning recipe designed for training on robot-native data. DreamFAR is significantly smaller than the high-performance video generation models, yet shows better understanding of contact and causality, and runs 10 FPS on a commercial GPU. Experimentally, DreamFAR significantly outperforms existing models in predicting the long-horizon future. We further demonstrate various applications where DreamFAR can be used, including policy evaluation and mixed-data co-training. Project page: https://www.yimingdou.com/DreamFAR/

papers.title: How Much Distribution Shift Can a Clustering Withstand? Exact Split and Merge Certificates for Structured Transports
papers.abstract: In clustering, the distribution of the population being clustered is often uncertain or changes over time, so the true distribution may shift away from the nominal distribution used to form the clustering. Once the clustering is committed and each member is assigned to a cluster, such shifts may change the distribution of each cluster. They can make a cluster too spread out for one representative at a given resolution, motivating a split, or bring distinct clusters close enough to share a representative at that resolution, motivating a merge. We make these split and merge events precise using a local stability criterion built on the phase-transition analysis in deterministic annealing. This notion of stability enables us to quantify how robust a clustering is against such events. Furthermore, motivated by applications in which uncertainty and population change are structured, we study shifts whose displacements are restricted to a prescribed subspace. The smallest structured shifts that reach the respective thresholds define the split and merge radii, for which we obtain exact semidefinite programming (SDP) reformulations. The split SDP has only two scalar decision variables. These convex reformulations enable us to combine the radii into a robustness certificate for the full clustering that gives the size of the smallest structured shift that reaches any monitored split or merge threshold.

papers.title: Transient Synchronization and Entanglement through Shared Dissipation in Circuit QED
papers.abstract: We propose a superconducting circuit in which two resonators couple through DC-biased SQUIDs to a common lossy auxiliary mode. Adiabatic elimination yields collective damping and correlated noise with an overlap $ξ$ whose magnitude is tuned by the flux biases and whose sign follows the relative sign of the couplings. The full three-mode dynamics confirm this reduced description. For detuned resonators, we derive the exceptional-point condition, above which the mean amplitudes lock to a common frequency. For resonant modes, unequal collective decay produces transient synchronization, antiphase or in phase depending on the relative sign of the couplings, with an analytical synchronization time set by the collective decay splitting and the initial mean amplitudes. For initially separable squeezed states, the same relaxation converts local squeezing into transient entanglement, quantified by logarithmic negativity. We obtain closed-form expressions for the squeezing threshold above which entanglement appears and for the time at which it disappears. Thermal noise suppresses entanglement without changing the mean-amplitude synchronization time at fixed parameters. For realistic circuit parameters, these effects occur within a few hundred nanoseconds and are accessible through output-field measurements. A single tunable shared channel thus produces an exceptional point, transient synchronization, and transient entanglement, and provides a controllable source of correlated noise for superconducting circuits.

papers.title: KV-LTM: Persistent Per-Session KV Caches as Long-Term Memory for Personal Assistants
papers.abstract: Personal assistants accumulate months of conversations, but today's long-term memory stacks put derivation or selection between a question and its evidence. In a system-level comparison on LongMemEval, two commercial assistants scored well below the same model reading the history offline [1], consistent with, but not isolating, content loss between write and read. We propose KV-LTM: a memory tier storing each session's raw text plus its KV cache under a fixed reader model, answering by restoring cached sessions and appending the question. KV-LTM is complementary to, not a replacement for, retrieval and indexing. Text is the memory of record; the cache is a recompute-free prefill accelerator, degrading gracefully to text. We specify the design: storage record, budget-derived retention, append-only read path, and bounded aggregation. We size it analytically: across pinned BF16 full-attention (GQA) and latent-cached MLA configurations, per-token state spans approximately 31K-328K bytes (the pinned KDA+MLA hybrid differs: approximately 8.1K bytes/token plus a fixed per-session recurrent term), giving approximately 0.34-3.6 TB per user-year at a declared 30K-token/day scenario, against approximately 49 MB of raw text; per-query cost is modelled as regime-conditional transfer, attention, decode, aggregation, and compute. We define an evaluation protocol needing no persistent-cache implementation for logical QA evaluation: per-session prefill emulates valid cache reuse under the same model/input-state contract and ideal arithmetic, with named arms, controlled baselines, and a preregistered reader-model gate; a separate minimal real-cache replay tests numerical equivalence and measures the cost axis, with outcomes not assumed. KV-LTM trades storage for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity, within a declared retention budget.

papers.title: Fundamental physics with quantum sensors in space
papers.abstract: Quantum sensors such as atomic clocks, atom interferometers, and atomic magnetometers can be used as sensitive probes of physics beyond the Standard Model. Space offers microgravity, long baselines, low environmental noise, access to varying gravitational potentials, and unique opportunities involving the Sun, Moon, planets, and asteroids. These proceedings of the Aspen Center for Physics workshop on "Fundamental physics in space with quantum sensors," held February 22-27, 2026, summarize the scientific case, current capabilities, and space mission concepts for investigating dark matter, testing general relativity, and detecting gravitational waves in frequency bands inaccessible from the ground.

papers.title: Beyond Appearance: Where Forest Visual Place Recognition Actually Fails
papers.abstract: Visual place recognition (VPR) in forest environments remains challenging because repetitive vegetation, and changes in illumination, season, and viewpoint can make distinct places appear similar and revisited places appear substantially different. In this paper, we investigate whether temporal, linguistic, structural, and geometric context can improve on an appearance-only descriptor, and what limits each representation when it does not. Using MegaLoc as the appearance-based baseline on the WildCross benchmark, we evaluate score-space and descriptor-space sequence matching, vision-language captions and reranking, scene-graph representations, and depth-derived stem graphs across same-direction revisits, extended routes, and reverse traversals. On a same-direction revisit, both sequence matching strategies reach similar Recall@1 (94.1% vs. 91.5%), but recall at 100% precision rises from 50.9% (single-frame MegaLoc) to 71.6% in score space and falls to 36.5% in descriptor space. The remaining context representations provide no consistent improvement over the appearance-based baseline. Same-place captions show limited place-specific discrimination, reranking is constrained by the initial candidate shortlist, and stem-graph matching remains weak even with LiDAR depth.

papers.title: Deciding Without Pointing: A Case Study of Whether a Decision Model Localizes the Anomalies It Detects
papers.abstract: Decision models can answer a typed question about an image with a probability per option, without generating text. In our case study of Clef-flash (post-trained Qwen3.5-9B backbone) on industrial inspection benchmarks, we ask whether it localizes the anomalies it detects. We obtained uneven results with zero-shot detection: per-category image AUROC 0.924 on MVTec AD and 0.668 on MVTec AD 2. On the former, the decision head's routing attention produces 0.391 mean per-image pixel AUROC, and hiding the image tokens from it leaves detection unchanged. The multimodal LLM's backbone attention does point at the defect, however it falls below a center prior when we change question. It falls below chance if we remove textual context in the question, partly due to backbone attention leaving the object, while the head's map hardly changes. The backbone's states carry the location when probed with normal images, on the test-split images, however, the decision depends on the defect region. A larger model, Clef, that comes with a post-trained Qwen3.8-27B backbone, gives no useful map in the decision head either. We found that it's possible to recover anomaly location by asking question specifically on an image region, retraining the head or reading the backbone, but none matches dedicated few-shot localizers.

papers.title: An alternate proof of the QMA lower bound for set-size estimation
papers.abstract: In the set-size estimation query task, a query algorithm decides whether an $N$-bit input has Hamming weight $\ge B$ or $\le A$ (with $\ge B$ as the yes instances and $\le A$ as the no instances). When $B = 2A$, this is sometimes called approximate counting. The query complexity for this problem with a quantum witness (i.e., $\mathsf{QMA}$ query bounds) was resolved by Aaronson, Kothari, Kretschmer, and Thaler (CCC 2020) and proved using Laurent polynomials. Here we give a morally similar but distinct proof of the lower bound using the polynomial method.

papers.title: DEFTS: Data-Efficient, Training-Free Few-Shot Learning for CLIP in the Text Subspace
papers.abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) achieves impressive zero-shot image classification performance by comparing image embeddings against class-specific text embeddings. While recent few-shot methods leverage labeled training samples to improve upon this zero-shot baseline, they often predominantly rely on image embeddings and underutilize the semantic structure of the text embeddings. In this paper, we introduce DEFTS, a data-efficient, training-free few-shot classification method strictly in the text subspace. We first demonstrate empirically that while raw text embeddings can be suboptimal as direct classifiers, the linear subspace they span remains highly discriminative. DEFTS therefore proposes to reduce the image-text modality gap by projecting estimated image prototypes directly into this subspace. Importantly, by expressing these prototypes as linear combinations of text embeddings, DEFTS reduces a high-dimensional estimation problem to the derivation of just a few coefficients. These coefficients are then computed via a Bayesian posterior mean, using a prior naturally centered on the original text embedding coordinates. Extensive experiments across 12 image classification benchmarks demonstrate that DEFTS significantly improves upon existing training-free methods.

papers.title: Accelerating auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo with mixed-precision random propagators
papers.abstract: We develop an algorithm to propagate auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) wavefunctions in mixed precision. We target NVIDIA Tensor Cores using the TensorFloat-32 (TF32) format. We approximate each full-precision array by a TF32 leading term and a TF32 residual, and each full-precision matrix product by three TF32 products accumulated in full precision. Benchmarks on hydrogen chains show that mixed-precision propagation is consistently faster than double-precision GPU propagation, with an increasing advantage as the system size grows. The resulting local-energy deviations remain small over the propagation windows considered here. These results identify the stochastic two-body propagator as a particularly effective target for reduced precision, while our method allows higher precision to be retained for accuracy-sensitive operations. Hence, our algorithm provides a practical way to speed up AFQMC calculations and demonstrates where reduced precision can be applied without adverse effects on the method's accuracy.

papers.title: High-Order Regularization for Singular and Nearly Singular Laplace and Stokes Layer Potentials in Two Dimensions
papers.abstract: Layer potentials represent the solutions of many elliptic boundary value problems, but their kernels have the singularity of the fundamental solution, so standard quadrature loses accuracy at targets on or near the boundary. In two dimensions, Gaussian regularization of the logarithmic kernel gives a smooth kernel involving the exponential integral $E_1$, but for the single layer its regularization error is only first order in the smoothing radius $δ$. We construct modified kernels for two-dimensional Laplace and Stokes single- and double-layer potentials that achieve regularization error $O(δ^p)$, $p=3,5,7$, uniformly for targets on and near the curve. The resulting method is both high-order accurate and easy to implement: the integrals are evaluated directly by the periodic trapezoidal rule on a single fixed set of boundary nodes for all targets. Choosing $δ=c h^q$ with $q<1$, where $h$ is the node spacing, keeps the discretization error smaller than the regularization error as $h\to0$, and numerical experiments confirm the predicted $O(h^{pq})$ convergence. Finally, we combine the near-curve evaluation with a fast Poisson solver to compute the potentials on the entire Cartesian grid.

papers.title: Hyperkähler Periods in Families of Parabolic Higgs Bundle Moduli Spaces
papers.abstract: We consider the period map on families of parabolic Higgs bundle moduli spaces with varying parabolic weights $α$ and Higgs field eigenvalues $σ$. We assemble the moduli spaces into a smooth family $π:\mathscr M\toΛ$ where $Λ$ encodes $(α,σ)$, and define parallel transport for homology along paths in an open dense subset $Λ_0\subsetΛ$. By generalizing a classical theorem of Duistermaat and Heckman, we prove that the period map is affine linear in $(α,σ)$, with slope governed by the curvature class of a principal torus bundle over $\mathscr M$. For the four-dimensional moduli spaces of types $E_6,E_7,E_8$, we compute these classes to get explicit formulas for the period maps.

papers.title: Orbital Stability and Instability of Slow and Fast Solitary Waves of gILW
papers.abstract: We study the solitary waves of the generalized Intermediate Long Wave equation (gILW), for a power-type nonlinearity of order $p\geq1$. Using concentration-compactness and symmetric rearrangement, we prove existence of suitable (even, strictly positive and radially decreasing) solitary waves of gILW for every $p\geq1$, and show that, as the depth parameter tends to infinity, they converge in the energy space and in $L^q$, $q\in[2,\infty]$, to the solitary waves of the generalized Benjamin-Ono equation (gBO), while, as the depth parameter tends to zero, after a suitable rescaling, they converge in $L^q$, $q\in[2,\infty]$, to the solitary waves of the generalized Korteweg-de Vries equation (gKdV). Our main results concern the orbital stability of slow and fast solitary waves of gILW, that is, of those for which the product $δc$ of the depth parameter and the velocity is small or large, respectively. For slow waves we obtain stability for $p=1,2,3$ and instability for $p\geq5$ (the same threshold as for gKdV), while for fast waves we obtain stability for $p=1$ and instability for $p\geq3$ (the same threshold as for gBO). In particular, for $p=3$ the stability of the solitary waves changes from one regime to the other. These results extend to $p>1$ the classical result of Albert, Bona and Henry for the Intermediate Long Wave equation ($p=1$). The proof proceeds by perturbation theory, transferring spectral information from gKdV and gBO to gILW through the convergence of the corresponding solitary-wave operators, and in particular avoids any use of an explicit formula for the solitary wave profile, none being available for $p>1$.

papers.title: Deep Learning Models for Fractional Option Pricing
papers.abstract: This paper investigates whether neural networks can infer fractional option prices and the Hurst parameter directly from sequences of fractional Gaussian returns, without separately estimating the latent parameters for each new sequence. Feedforward neural networks (FNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are trained to jointly predict European call prices, put prices, and the Hurst parameter from 252-return sequences. A controlled simulation varies the total sample size from 5,000 to 500,000 sequences and evaluates point prediction, empirical residual-based prediction intervals, and computational performance. The neural-network models are also compared on a common simulated test set with Bayesian joint estimation and exact Gaussian maximum likelihood estimation. In that four-method comparison, the LSTM achieves the lowest Hurst-parameter root mean squared error (0.033) and option-price root mean squared error (1.305). After training, neural-network predictions are substantially faster than repeated parameter estimation, although the methods quantify uncertainty in different ways. Applications to five financial return series illustrate differences between data-driven and model-based fractional price estimates. The results support sequence-based learning as a computationally efficient complement to statistical inference under the assumed fractional model; they do not establish out-of-distribution accuracy or accuracy against observed traded-option prices.

papers.title: Safe Reinforcement Learning with Hard Constraints: Policy Gradient Methods with Intersample Guarantees
papers.abstract: We develop a policy-gradient (PG) reinforcement learning (RL) framework with hard inter-sample control barrier function (CBF)-based safety constraints for nonlinear sampled-data systems. We first design a class of stochastic policies with support truncated to sampling-period-dependent safe control sets, that guarantee safety-by-construction at sampling instants. We then propose a model-free PG algorithm that searches over the class of safe-by-design policies and establish sufficient conditions on sampling-period such that any action sampled from safe control sets remains safe throughout the sampling interval, providing inter-sample guarantees. We further establish finite-time convergence and sample complexity guarantees for the proposed PG algorithm and characterize its global optimality under gradient dominance. Finally, we illustrate inter-sample safety guarantees on a safe quadrotor navigation environment.

papers.title: Unveiling the infrared excess of SIPS J2045-6332 II: SPHEREx spectral decomposition supports a young unresolved binary interpretation
papers.abstract: SIPS J2045-6332 is an unusual low-mass object previously identified by its infrared excess and possible signatures of youth and unresolved multiplicity. Earlier work suggested that it is relatively young and may host a mid-L companion. Here we reassess the system using low-resolution 0.75-5 micron spectroscopy from SPHEREx. We perform single- and binary-template spectral decomposition with field-gravity and intermediate-gravity (beta) templates spanning M8-L4. Binary-template models consistently outperform single-template models, most strongly for the beta templates. The preferred solution, an L0beta + L1beta combination (reduced chi^2 = 10.72), best matches the combined-light spectrum, although M9beta + L1beta and M9beta + L2beta give comparably good fits. Combining bolometric luminosities from gravity-dependent bolometric corrections (log L/Lsun = -3.42 +/- 0.08 and -3.85 +/- 0.09) with the Sonora evolutionary models, we estimate component masses of ~0.015 and ~0.011 Msun at 25 Myr and >~0.043-0.046 and ~0.038-0.043 Msun at 200-250 Myr for the primary and secondary (primary values are lower limits), implying a mass ratio q <~ 0.7-0.9, i.e. a companion of comparable but not necessarily equal mass. These results independently reinforce previous interpretations that SIPS J2045-6332 is a relatively young unresolved binary, and demonstrate the capability of SPHEREx spectroscopy to characterise young low-mass binaries through spectral decomposition.

papers.title: First-Order Model-Free Policy Gradient for Undiscounted LQR with Global Optimality and Convergence Guarantees
papers.abstract: We provide a first-order model-free policy gradient (PG) framework for learning undiscounted infinite-horizon linear quadratic regulator (LQR) policies with global optimality and convergence guarantees. We first construct a stochastic wrapper policy class parameterized by the LQR gain to enable exploration around a deterministic linear control law. We analyze the additional cost induced by exploration over infinite-horizon, and establish a weak gradient dominance condition that characterizes global optimality under exploration. We then construct a model-free first-order PG algorithm using sampled trajectory information, without identifying the dynamics or approximating a value function. Finally, we establish finite-time convergence guarantees, providing the sufficient number of samples required for near-global optimality with our proposed PG algorithms.

papers.title: From Apology to Action: Apologies, Compensation, and Cooperation in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can make decisions that affect other agents, but what happens after a harmful or unsuccessful interaction remains poorly understood. We investigate whether apologies by LLM agents are associated with subsequent cooperative behaviour, using controlled Prisoner's Dilemma experiments with four commercial models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and Mistral Large 3). Across payoff conditions, we examine when agents apologise, the reasons they provide, and the actions that follow. We also examine how access to one round of interaction history affects behaviour and, in a second experiment, whether and how agents offer compensation alongside their apologies. Apology behaviour differed substantially across models and preceding interaction outcomes, and verbal expressions of cooperation did not always align with subsequent actions. Notably, Claude Opus 4.8 apologised even after mutual cooperation, while Mistral Large 3 apologised after being exploited but continued to defect even when its opponent cooperated. After unilateral defection, positively compensated apologies from GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro were followed by mutual cooperation, unlike those from Claude and Mistral. Our findings suggest that apologies, compensation, and strategic behaviour are distinct: conciliatory messages may precede continued defection, while costly apologies may go unanswered. This has important implications for the study of machine behaviour and human-AI interactions, as verbal signals alone may not reliably reflect an AI system's subsequent actions.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Nonlinear Dynamical Systems: The Three Clocks of Depth, Training, and Generation
papers.abstract: Language models are dynamical systems. A transformer is iterated over its layers, over the steps of its training and over the tokens it generates, and on each of these three clocks it shows behavior that nonlinear dynamics has studied for a century: fixed points, bifurcations, synchronization, chaos and noise-driven escape from potential wells. The two communities rarely meet, so this behavior is often rediscovered under new names. We build a bridge between them. To describe, we condense about 200 papers into the Three-Clock Dictionary, which maps fifteen concepts of nonlinear dynamics onto each clock and marks every correspondence as proved, measured or conjectured, and we show each concept in a mechanical system and in a language model side by side. To explain, we derive reduced-order models: the softmax is a Boltzmann distribution, gradient descent an Euler step on a nonlinear spring, a loss spike a ball thrown out of a stiff valley, attention on the circle a Kuramoto model, and a repetition loop a well that deepens while it is occupied. We then test these explanations on open language models, on a laptop CPU. Escape from repetition loops in GPT-2 and Pythia follows the Arrhenius law with the logit gap as the barrier, and the barrier deepens and then saturates, so the temperature needed to leave a loop falls like $1/\ln N$ with the generation length $N$ and rises with model size. Coherent text lives in a narrow window of temperatures, which a small reasoning model shares at its recommended temperature. Training makes each Pythia layer more expansive, and a small transformer trains at a multi-mode edge of stability. The third step, solving problems of language models, is still ahead: controllers derived from the escape analysis remove loops but do not yet beat the best fixed temperature. We state twelve open problems where nonlinear dynamics could get there.

papers.title: Emerging Vertical Power Delivery in AI Data Centers: Challenges and Solutions
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) workloads is increasing power demand in AI data centers, and processor current is projected to reach 2000 A and beyond. This trend is exposing the limitations of lateral power delivery (LPD) to processors and has motivated growing interest in vertical power delivery (VPD). This paper reviews the power delivery network (PDN) of AI data centers and the upcoming transition from LPD to VPD. First, the 800 VDC power delivery architecture, the impedance behavior of the PDN, and the limitations of LPD are discussed. Then, VPD implementation approaches, reported converter designs, and packaging technologies are examined, together with integrated voltage regulators (IVRs) and embedded passive components. In addition, power integrity simulations are presented to compare regulator and plane positions, from which a set of PDN design guidelines is derived. The results show that moving a voltage regulator module (VRM) from 50 mm away to directly below the die reduces the loop inductance by nearly half. In a complete PDN, this relocation lowers the low-frequency anti-resonant peak, whereas the mid- and high-frequency impedance depends on the decoupling stages and the position of the power and ground planes. This paper also shows that achieving practical VPD remains closely tied to challenges such as regulator height, passive-component embedding, and thermal management.

papers.title: Who Gets the Grid Capacity? Allocating Dynamic Access Among Multiple Virtual Power Plants
papers.abstract: Virtual power plants (VPPs) trade in the same wholesale market and share distribution lines and transformers, and uncoordinated, profit-maximizing VPPs can push a shared transformer past its thermal limit or drive a feeder voltage out of band. The utility, which only observes the front-of-the-meter net injection at each bus, must keep the network safe from that net injection alone. We allocate a 24-hour active and reactive operating envelope to each VPP by a Benders decomposition: the utility sets a trial envelope, each VPP solves its private convex portfolio problem, and the returned value and dual gradient become supporting cuts that rebuild its value function while its schedule, state, and cost stay private. The envelope carries the transformer's thermal state across hours, bounds a joint conditional value-at-risk over forecast uncertainty, and is re-optimized each hour with the current hour committed. On a reduced IEEE-13 feeder with real load and prices, an active-power-only implementation lowers the transformer's peak-temperature CVaR from 254 to 97\,$^\circ$C at a 28\% value give-up and holds the transformer below its limit where nameplate access breaches it.

papers.title: Modeling Document and Section Hierarchies in Embedding Space
papers.abstract: Embedded topic models integrate word embeddings into the topic generation process, producing coherent topics and robust performance on large vocabularies. However, each document is represented by a single topic distribution, ignoring its internal structure. Many real world collections, including legal documents, company and government reports, and online discussion forums, exhibit hierarchical organization in which documents consist of multiple sections that often address distinct subtopics. We introduce the Hierarchical Embedded Topic Model (hETM), a structured topic model that couples the topic distribution of a document and those of its sections through a hierarchical prior in the embedding space. We derive an amortized variational inference procedure for hETM and evaluate it on structured collections from each of these domains. Experimental results show that hETM achieves the lowest or near-lowest held-out perplexity among flat and hierarchical topic model baselines, along with comparable or higher topic quality. It also performs strongly on a downstream clustering task, achieving the best clustering performance on most of the collections.

papers.title: Laplacian Eigenvectors of Generically Weighted Graphs Have Pairwise Distinct Coordinates
papers.abstract: Poignard, Pereira and Pade conjectured that, for a generic choice of the nonzero weights of a given graph, the Fiedler vector of the weighted Laplacian has pairwise distinct coordinates. We give a proof that also covers every nonconstant eigenvector. For each connected graph on n vertices we construct a nonzero homogeneous polynomial with integer coefficients in the edge weights, of degree n(n-1)(n^2-n+2)/4, which vanishes at a positive weighting exactly when the Laplacian has a repeated eigenvalue, an eigenvector with a zero coordinate, or a nonconstant eigenvector with two equal coordinates. The exceptional weights therefore lie in an algebraic hypersurface, which gives structural genericity in the sense of Poignard, Pereira and Pade; algebraically independent weights are never exceptional, and there are good integer weights not exceeding the degree plus one. The polynomial is a product of Krylov determinants. Its nonvanishing follows by induction on trees: when a leaf is attached with a small weight, a cut identity gives the first-order profile of the new eigenvector and separates the coordinates that coincide in the limit. Exact small cases show that exceptional weightings need not be symmetric.

papers.title: WebAgents: Unbundling Agent Creation, Hosting, and Execution for an Agent-Native Web
papers.abstract: Large language models are moving from isolated assistants toward autonomous agents that can plan, use tools, and coordinate with others, motivating an emerging Agentic Web of independently developed agents and services. Realizing this vision requires agent behavior to move across creators, hosts, and runtimes without coupling publication to a particular execution environment or transferring authority over user resources. We introduce WebAgents, which unbundles these roles through a signed agent.pkg that carries portable workflows, skills, schemas, and resource requirements. An OpenClaw-based agent-native browser/runtime verifies the package, obtains authorization, and binds it at run time to user-controlled models, tools, permissions, and budgets, while hosts distribute the public program and may retain private services server-side. We demonstrate this contract with three unrelated workflows executed unchanged under local and API-backed models, including literature review with live services and a website-published travel agent using semantic tools and user-selected personal resources. In a controlled suite, WebAgents explicitly blocks all 716 injected contract violations while accepting all 295 matched benign controls, with median automated pre-execution processing below 0.5 s for all three packages. We conclude by outlining a path toward NANDA-based discovery and interoperable package ecosystems while retaining execution authority in the user's runtime.

papers.title: Synchrony, Affect, and Perceived Autonomy in Virtual Robot-Facilitated Anxiety Support Groups
papers.abstract: Socially assistive robots could expand access to group-based mental health support when skilled human facilitators are unavailable. However, their effectiveness will depend on whether they foster productive interactions among participants. We examined dyadic head-movement synchrony among 96 participants across 18 virtual robot-facilitated anxiety support group sessions. A human-controlled virtual robot, via a Wizard-of-Oz (WoZ) system, facilitated all sessions. We found that stronger peak synchrony predicted lower post-session negative affect. In contrast, speakers who more often followed listeners' movements reported higher negative affect and state anxiety, demonstrating that synchrony strength and direction capture distinct interpersonal processes. Participants who believed the robot was autonomous showed more genuine synchrony and stronger peaks than those who believed it was human-operated; more negative attitudes toward robots also predicted greater synchrony. These findings support synchrony as an objective, behaviorally grounded measure for evaluating robot-facilitated groups and a potential signal for guiding future autonomous facilitators.

papers.title: Sparse Integer Fourier Transform and Its Application In Machine Learning
papers.abstract: The Discrete Fourier transform, mainly implemented by Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), has been essential for numerous domains, such as digital signal processing and feature extraction in materials design. However, current FFT methods suffer from extensive non-trivial multiplications and twiddle-factor operations in the big data era. To improve the computational efficiency of FFT, this study proposes Sparse Integer Fourier Transform (SIFT), a method that leverages the fast computing of sparsity and small integers, and applies the Radix-n method to derive an FFT. The 2N-point DFT matrix in Radix-n FFT is decomposed into four sparse integer matrices. A diagonal matrix containing complex twiddle factors is efficiently approximated using an optimization strategy while the remaining matrices retain sparsity and integer entries. For radix-32 FFT, SIFT reduces the estimated arithmetic cost by 75%, with RMSE below $2.3765\times10^{-8}$ and MAPE below 0.01089%. We evaluate frequency extraction in a numerical test and an engineering case. In the numerical test, MAPE and RMSE are below 2.016% and $2.536\times10^{-6}$, respectively. For wind turbine fault diagnosis, SIFT extracts compact spectral features that retain fault information while reducing the classifier's input dimensionality relative to the full time series.

papers.title: Pathology Randomization for Synthetic Priors and Zero-Shot Detection
papers.abstract: Hospital brain imaging archives hold a diverse array of pathology at sample sizes beyond prospective studies, particularly for underrepresented populations and diseases. To unlock uncurated clinical data and scale analysis, methods are needed to detect abnormalities across contrasts and resolutions. Synthetic data has provided robust, contrast-agnostic models for a variety of human neuroimaging tasks in healthy anatomy, but pathology detection and other tasks in clinical settings still require real patient data, contrast-specific models, or disease-specific generators. We propose PathoDraw, a generative model of brain MRI with pathology. A conditional distribution of lesions given the healthy anatomy is drawn into the label map before contrast-agnostic rendering, and a single network estimates healthy anatomy with exact signed intensity deviation of any input scan. The contrast-agnostic 3D UNet learns the healthy labels under the lesion and the signed deviation directly and identifies pathology via robust tissue statistics and learned features, despite no training on real pathology. We show zero-shot detection on public stroke, tumor, and white matter hyperintensity datasets as well as archived clinical data, spanning $T_1$w, FLAIR and $T_2$w at various resolutions under a recent unsupervised anomaly detection benchmark protocol. Our single model exceeds or performs comparably to contrast-specific anomaly detectors trained on real scans and keeps healthy anatomy intact. The same generator trains networks for super-resolution and for registration in the presence of pathology. Our model, robust across acquisition and disease, enables the use of uncurated, archived data for clinical analysis. Our code is available at https://github.com/agr78/Pathology-Randomizer.

papers.title: Beyond Bitwidth: Deployment-Constrained Mixed-Precision Quantization for Multilingual LLM Inference on NVIDIA Blackwell
papers.abstract: Low-bit LLM quantization is useful only if a model preserves service-relevant accuracy, executes through supported GPU kernels, and meets measured memory and latency limits. We study Qwen3-8B on NVIDIA B200 with vLLM, including INT2/INT3, GPTQ, NVFP4, and mixed-precision configurations. We verify native packed execution and precision on all 144 fused linear modules and evaluate Korean, English, numerical, and reasoning quality under preregistered gates. Packed INT2 and INT3 execute, but all seven tested INT2 grids degenerate on generation. Isolated module-restoration effects are strongly non-additive; Korean and reasoning sensitivity rankings disagree, and a promising INT4/INT8 development candidate fails independent final evaluation. A configuration with 16-bit activations, 98 NVFP4 weight-only modules, 46 INT8 modules, and an INT8 output head passes all gates on the untouched FINAL-81 set (5,168 items): 5.917 GiB of weight-loading memory (limit 5.98), Korean teacher-correct retention 0.904 (gate 0.90), and TPOT ratio 0.939 relative to BF16. It improves paired accuracy over NVFP4 W4A4 by +1.4 percentage points (Bonferroni-adjusted interval [+0.2, +2.6]), compared with +3.4 points on the selection set. This comparison changes both activation precision and INT8 protection; exploratory analyses suggest that the activation change contributes substantially, but the isolated allocation effect is not established. Final checkpoints were not retained, and bitwise rebuild reproducibility remains unverified.

papers.title: How Many Persistent Features Does a Biometric Need? A Law Linking Equal Error Rate to Feature Count and Persistence
papers.abstract: A biometric designer controls the number of features and their temporal persistence. Earlier empirical work linked the equal error rate (EER) to persistence and to the required number of features by straight lines. We derive the law behind these regularities. For $N$ independent standardized Gaussian features with test-retest correlation $ρ$, scored by cosine similarity, Fisher's $z$-transform turns the genuine and impostor scores into two normals, giving $\mathrm{EER}=Φ(-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{N}\,\operatorname{atanh}ρ)$ and, inversely, $N=(2q/\operatorname{atanh}ρ)^2$ with $q=Φ^{-1}(1-\mathrm{EER})$; intercorrelated features enter through an effective count $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$. The central extension lets persistence vary across comparisons with spread $τ$ on Fisher's scale: $\mathrm{EER}=Φ(-m/(\sqrt{τ^2+v}+\sqrt{v}))$ with $v=1/(N_{\mathrm{eff}}-2)$, which for a normal spread has a floor $Φ(-m/τ)$ that no number of features can lower. With no fitted parameter the simple law reproduces published simulations and the EER-ICC line, and predicts the KCC-EER relation of eye-movement embeddings on GazeBase ($R^2=0.88$), though less well on GazeBaseVR ($0.63$). Read from the genuine and impostor scores, the general form matches the EER of eye movements, keystroke dynamics, the ECG and face embeddings over 101 conditions with $R^2=0.98$ and a median error of $0.6$ points, against $0.87$ and $1.9$ points for the simple law. The 61 eye-movement, keystroke and ECG conditions check consistency on the same scores; the 40 face conditions use held-out subjects, with the same accuracy. The product $τ\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{eff}}-2}$ gives a design rule: adding or decorrelating features pays fully while it is well below one and little once it exceeds about three, where only higher or more uniform persistence helps.

papers.title: Photonic Maxwells demon as an energy resource
papers.abstract: We propose a new realization of Maxwells demon for photons and its use as an energy resource. The starting point is a multilayer dielectric mirror that transmits photons within a certain wavelength band but reflects photons at longer wavelengths, followed by a material that irreversibly converts the wavelength. A 3D box constructed from these one-way mirrors is a self-acting Maxwells demon for photons. The first case considered is a one-way mirror for visible photons, converting blue to red as an example. The next case is a one-way mirror that transmits visible light but reflects infrared light, followed by a perfect blackbody.
